Data exfiltration to an external staging server
Lateral movement scanning across internal subnets

events.name: Sysmon service state changed
events.description: Reports when the Sysmon service itself starts or stops. Low signal on its own, but its presence marks the boundaries of Sysmon telemetry coverage on a host.

key_fields.meaning: Started or Stopped.
The Sysmon binary version running.
The event schema version, which determines which fields later events will contain.

events.normal_baseline: Fires once at every system boot when the Sysmon service starts, and again only if the service is deliberately stopped, upgraded, or reconfigured.
events.sample_log:
Sysmon service state changed:
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 06:15:02.004
State: Started
Version: 15.15
SchemaVersion: 4.90
anomalies: A Stopped state with no corresponding scheduled maintenance or upgrade, especially followed by a gap before the next Started event
A gap in Sysmon-generated events between a Stopped and a later Started state, indicating a window where logging was blind
Version or SchemaVersion downgrades, which can indicate an attacker reinstalling an older Sysmon build with fewer event types

attack_example.scenario: An attacker with local admin rights stops the Sysmon service to blind logging before dropping tooling, then never restarts it, leaving a permanent coverage gap.
attack_example.log:
Sysmon service state changed:
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:00:47.220
State: Stopped
Version: 15.15
SchemaVersion: 4.90

investigation_steps: Check what account and process stopped the service by pulling the corresponding Service Control Manager event (7036) or Security 4688 for sc.exe/net.exe stop commands issued around the same UtcTime.
Establish the exact gap window between this Stopped event and the next Started event, and treat that window as a logging blind spot requiring other data sources.
Confirm the service was intended to be stopped (patch window, planned reconfig) against a change ticket before ruling it benign.
false_positives: Planned Sysmon version upgrades or configuration deployments that briefly stop and restart the service
Endpoint agent reinstallation during routine imaging or patch cycles
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 4
| where State == "Stopped"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, State, Version, SchemaVersion
related_attacks: Defense evasion via disabling host-based logging before further malicious activity
Anti-forensic gaps created ahead of ransomware deployment

events.name: Process terminated
events.description: Reports when a monitored process exits. On its own it carries little detection value, but paired with the matching Sysmon-1 event it lets an analyst compute exact process lifetime and confirm when a suspicious process actually stopped running.

key_fields.meaning: Matches the ProcessGuid from this process's original Sysmon-1 event, used to close out its lifetime.
The executable that terminated.
The account context the process ran under.

events.normal_baseline: Generated continuously as every process on the system exits normally; volume roughly matches Sysmon-1 volume.
events.sample_log:
Process terminated:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 08:24:10.665
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-1e35-66f0-3701-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 6820
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
User: CORP\jsmith
anomalies: A short-lived process (seconds of runtime between its Sysmon-1 and this event) matching a known LOLBin abuse pattern, suggesting a quick payload execution and cleanup
Security or monitoring tooling processes terminating unexpectedly outside of a maintenance window
A process terminating immediately after a Sysmon-8 CreateRemoteThread or Sysmon-25 ProcessTampering event targeting it

attack_example.scenario: The PowerShell process used to retrieve a Stage-2 payload exits within seconds of launch, consistent with a fire-and-forget downloader script.
attack_example.log:
Process terminated:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:05:41.030
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2e13-66f0-4a02-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 9144
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
User: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Join to the corresponding Sysmon-1 event by ProcessGuid to compute process lifetime and confirm whether it matches a known short-lived-downloader pattern.
If the terminated process is security-relevant (AV, EDR agent, logging service), check for a preceding kill command or privilege escalation.
Use the termination timestamp as the closing boundary when building an incident timeline for this ProcessGuid.
false_positives: Normal short-lived utility processes (ipconfig, whoami, findstr) that legitimately run for milliseconds
Scheduled tasks and scripts that intentionally spawn and exit quickly as part of routine automation
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and (EventID == 1 or EventID == 5)
| summarize Started=minif(EventID==1, TimeGenerated), Terminated=minif(EventID==5, TimeGenerated) by ProcessGuid, Image
| extend LifetimeSeconds = datetime_diff('second', Terminated, Started)
| where LifetimeSeconds between (0 .. 3) and Image has "powershell.exe"
related_attacks: Fire-and-forget downloader scripts used in staged malware delivery
Security tooling termination as part of defense evasion

events.name: Driver loaded
events.description: Logged whenever a kernel driver is loaded, along with its hash and signature status. Signature verification runs asynchronously, so SignatureStatus may briefly show as unavailable even for legitimate drivers.

key_fields.meaning: Full path of the driver file (.sys) that was loaded.
Whether the driver is digitally signed, who signed it, and whether the signature validated.
Hashes of the driver file, used to match against known-malicious or known-vulnerable driver hash lists.

events.normal_baseline: Occurs at boot for built-in Windows drivers and periodically for hardware, VPN, antivirus, and virtualization drivers being loaded or updated.
events.sample_log:
Driver loaded:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 06:15:19.310
ImageLoaded: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\dam.sys
Hashes: SHA1=4A5B6C7D8E9F0A1B2C3D4E5F60718293A4B5C6D,MD5=8F1E2D3C4B5A69708C1D2E3F4A5B6C70,SHA256=6D8E0F2B4C6E8A0D2F4B6E8A0D2C4E6B8D0F2A4C6E8B0D2F4A6C8E0B2D4F6A8C,IMPHASH=B2C3D4E5F60718293A4B5C6D7E8F90A1
Signed: true
Signature: Microsoft Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher
SignatureStatus: Valid
anomalies: An unsigned driver, or one with SignatureStatus of Invalid, loaded on a production endpoint
A known-vulnerable signed driver being loaded shortly before other suspicious kernel-level activity (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver abuse)
A driver loaded from a user-writable path such as AppData or a temp directory instead of System32\drivers
Driver hash matching a public threat-intel list of malicious or vulnerable driver hashes

attack_example.scenario: An attacker loads a legitimately signed but known-vulnerable driver to gain kernel-level primitives for disabling EDR, a BYOVD technique used by multiple ransomware crews.
attack_example.log:
Driver loaded:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:10:02.885
ImageLoaded: C:\Windows\Temp\rtcore64.sys
Hashes: SHA1=9C8B7A6F5E4D3C2B1A0F9E8D7C6B5A4938271605,MD5=1A2B3C4D5E6F70819A2B3C4D5E6F7081,SHA256=A0B2C4D6E8F00A2C4E6B8D0F2A4C6E8B0D2F4A6C8E0B2D4F6A8C0E2B4D6F8A0C,IMPHASH=C3D4E5F60718293A4B5C6D7E8F90A1B2
Signed: true
Signature: Micro-Star International CO., LTD.
SignatureStatus: Valid

investigation_steps: Check ImageLoaded's file path; drivers loaded from Temp, Downloads, or other user-writable locations are inherently suspicious regardless of signature.
Match the driver hash against known vulnerable-driver lists (e.g. LOLDrivers) even when SignatureStatus shows Valid, since BYOVD abuses legitimately signed drivers.
Look for immediately following Sysmon-10 ProcessAccess or process/service tampering events consistent with EDR-killing behavior after the driver loads.
false_positives: Legitimate hardware and peripheral drivers installed by IT during routine provisioning
Asynchronous signature verification lag causing a momentary SignatureStatus of Unavailable on a genuinely valid driver

attack_techniques.name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service

events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 6
| where Signed == false or ImageLoaded has_any ("\\Temp\\", "\\Downloads\\", "\\AppData\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ImageLoaded, Signed, Signature, SignatureStatus, Hashes
related_attacks: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) EDR-killing campaigns
Rootkit installation for persistence and stealth
Ransomware precursor activity disabling security tooling

events.name: Image loaded
events.description: Logs when a DLL or other module is loaded into a process, disabled by default because enabling it for all processes generates enormous volume. It's most useful when scoped with filters to specific processes of interest for catching DLL side-loading and injected module loads.

key_fields.meaning: The process the module was loaded into.
Full path of the DLL that was loaded.
Whether the loaded module is signed and whether that signature validated.
Hash of the loaded module for reputation matching.

events.normal_baseline: Every process loads dozens to hundreds of legitimate system and application DLLs during normal startup and operation; this is why the event is disabled by default.
events.sample_log:
Image loaded:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 11:02:44.190
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-5c01-66f0-1a02-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 4820
Image: C:\Program Files\VendorApp\app.exe
ImageLoaded: C:\Windows\System32\version.dll
FileVersion: 10.0.19041.1

SignatureStatus: Valid
User: CORP\jsmith

An unsigned or invalidly signed DLL loaded into a high-value process such as lsass.exe or a browser process
A vendor-signed executable loading an unsigned DLL placed alongside it in the same folder shortly after that DLL was written to disk

attack_example.scenario: A legitimate, signed application executable is placed in a temp folder alongside a malicious DLL with the exact filename the app expects, causing the app to side-load attacker code under a trusted process.

User: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Compare ImageLoaded's directory against the expected install path for that DLL name; a system DLL name loaded from a temp or user directory is a strong side-loading indicator.
Check the loaded DLL's Sysmon-11 FileCreate event to see when and by what process it was written to disk relative to when the host executable ran.
Verify Signed/SignatureStatus on the DLL itself, since side-loaded payloads are typically unsigned even when the host executable is legitimately signed.
false_positives: Plugin or extension architectures that legitimately load third-party unsigned DLLs by design
Portable applications that ship their own copies of common system DLL names for compatibility reasons
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 7
| where Signed == false and ImageLoaded has_any ("\\Temp\\", "\\AppData\\Local\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, ImageLoaded, Signed, SignatureStatus
related_attacks: DLL side-loading for defense evasion and persistence
Reflective DLL injection payload delivery
Trusted-process masquerading via legitimate signed host binaries

events.name: CreateRemoteThread
events.description: Detects when one process creates a thread inside another process, the classic mechanism behind DLL injection, reflective loading, and code-injection-based process hiding. StartModule and StartFunction are inferred from the start address and can be empty if it falls outside known loaded modules.

key_fields.meaning: The process that created the thread and the process it was created in.
The memory address the new thread begins executing at.
The module and exported function inferred to correspond to StartAddress, often empty for shellcode running from unmapped or unbacked memory.
The thread ID created in the target process.

events.normal_baseline: Rare in normal operation outside of legitimate debuggers, some security products, and certain application frameworks that use cross-process threading deliberately.
events.sample_log:
CreateRemoteThread detected:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:15:22.740
SourceProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2e13-66f0-4a02-000000000a00}
SourceProcessId: 9144

TargetProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-7a01-66f0-1101-000000000a00}
TargetProcessId: 2244

NewThreadId: 8812
StartAddress: 0x0000021A3F4B0000
StartModule: -
StartFunction: -
SourceUser: CORP\k.patel
TargetUser: CORP\k.patel
anomalies: Empty StartModule and StartFunction, indicating the thread starts in unbacked or unmapped memory rather than a known DLL export (shellcode)
A scripting engine or office process (powershell.exe, winword.exe) as SourceImage injecting into an unrelated process
TargetImage is a commonly abused injection target such as explorer.exe, svchost.exe, or a browser process
SourceUser and TargetUser differing, suggesting cross-session or cross-privilege injection

attack_example.scenario: An implant injects a reflective loader thread into notepad.exe to run its payload inside a benign-looking process and evade process-based detection.
attack_example.log:

RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:15:22.740
SourceProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2e13-66f0-4a02-000000000a00}
SourceProcessId: 9144

TargetProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-7a01-66f0-1101-000000000a00}
TargetProcessId: 2244

NewThreadId: 8812
StartAddress: 0x0000021A3F4B0000
StartModule: -
StartFunction: -
SourceUser: CORP\k.patel
TargetUser: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Check whether StartAddress falls inside any module loaded in TargetImage; an address outside all loaded modules strongly suggests injected shellcode.
Pull TargetImage's Sysmon-1 creation event and subsequent Sysmon-3 network activity to see if it began behaving abnormally after the injection.
Review SourceImage's own parent chain and recent file writes for the dropper or loader that performed the injection.
false_positives: Legitimate debuggers and diagnostic tools (Visual Studio, WinDbg, Process Explorer) that intentionally create remote threads
Some enterprise security and monitoring agents that inject hooking threads into monitored processes by design
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 8
| where isempty(StartModule) and isempty(StartFunction)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SourceImage, TargetImage, StartAddress, SourceUser

Cross-process code execution used by credential-theft toolkits

events.name: RawAccessRead
events.description: Detects when a process reads directly from a disk or volume using the \\.\ device path notation, bypassing the normal file system API. This is a common technique for reading files locked for normal access, dumping raw disk data for exfiltration, or evading file-access auditing.

key_fields.meaning: The disk or volume device path being read directly, e.g. \Device\HarddiskVolume2.
The process performing the raw read.

events.normal_baseline: Legitimate disk imaging, backup, defragmentation, and forensic tools are the primary normal source of this event; it is otherwise rare on an endpoint.
events.sample_log:
RawAccessRead detected:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 12:30:18.442
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-8b01-66f0-1201-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 5100
Image: C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe
Device: \Device\HarddiskVolume2
User: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
anomalies: A user-mode process with no legitimate disk-imaging or backup role performing raw volume reads
Raw reads targeting the volume containing NTDS.dit or the SAM/SYSTEM registry hives, consistent with offline credential extraction
Raw reads immediately preceding large outbound network transfers from the same host

attack_example.scenario: An attacker reads the raw NTDS.dit-containing volume directly to bypass file locks and extract Active Directory credential material without touching the file through the normal API.
attack_example.log:
RawAccessRead detected:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:20:07.318
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-9c02-66f0-2202-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 6604
Image: C:\Windows\Temp\ntdsutil_dump.exe
Device: \Device\HarddiskVolume1
User: CORP\svc_backup

investigation_steps: Identify which volume the Device path corresponds to and whether it hosts sensitive data such as NTDS.dit, SAM, or SYSTEM hives.
Check whether Image is a known, approved backup/imaging tool; an unrecognized binary performing raw reads warrants immediate escalation.
Look for follow-on Sysmon-11 file writes or Sysmon-3 network connections from the same process indicating exfiltration of the extracted data.
false_positives: Approved backup and disk-imaging software (Veeam, wbadmin, forensic tools) operating on their normal schedule
Disk defragmentation and disk-health utilities that read raw volume structures

Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 9
| where Image !has_any ("wbengine.exe", "vssvc.exe", "defrag.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, Device, User
related_attacks: Offline Active Directory credential extraction via NTDS.dit theft
Anti-forensic reads bypassing file-access auditing
Ransomware volume-level data staging before encryption

events.name: ProcessAccess
events.description: Logs when one process opens a handle to another, an operation typically followed by reading or writing that process's memory. This is the primary Sysmon event for catching LSASS credential dumping, since tools like Mimikatz must first open a handle to lsass.exe before scraping its memory.

key_fields.meaning: The process opening the handle and the process being accessed.
The hex access mask granted; 0x1010 or 0x1fffff-style broad access rights to a sensitive process like lsass.exe are the key thing to flag.
The module+offset call stack that led to the access, useful for spotting known credential-dumping tool signatures.

events.normal_baseline: High volume overall from legitimate diagnostic tools (Task Manager, Process Explorer, monitoring agents) that routinely open handles to query process state; must be filtered heavily to be useful.

SourceUser: CORP\jsmith
TargetUser: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
anomalies: GrantedAccess of 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) or 0x1410 to lsass.exe from a process other than a recognized security or diagnostic tool
SourceImage running from a temp or user-writable directory with an unusual name accessing lsass.exe or another security process
CallTrace showing modules associated with known credential-dumping tools or reflectively loaded, unbacked memory regions
A burst of ProcessAccess events against lsass.exe from the same SourceImage in rapid succession

Check SourceImage's file path, signature, and Sysmon-1 command line for signs of a renamed or repackaged credential-dumping tool.
If confirmed malicious, treat every credential on that host as compromised and pivot to look for follow-on 4624/4648 logons using those credentials elsewhere.
false_positives: Endpoint security products and diagnostic utilities that legitimately and routinely open handles to lsass.exe
Windows Error Reporting or crash-dump utilities briefly accessing a crashed process

Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 10
| where TargetImage has "lsass.exe" and GrantedAccess in ("0x1fffff", "0x1410", "0x1010")
| where SourceImage !has_any ("Taskmgr.exe", "procexp", "MsMpEng.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SourceImage, GrantedAccess, SourceUser

Pass-the-Hash and Pass-the-Ticket follow-on attacks
Comsvcs.dll MiniDump abuse against lsass.exe

events.name: FileCreate
events.description: Logged whenever a file is created or overwritten. Extremely useful for watching autostart locations, download and temp directories, and other common malware-drop paths where the earliest evidence of a payload landing on disk appears.

key_fields.meaning: Full path of the file that was created or overwritten.
The process that created the file.
The timestamp the file was created at, useful as a baseline to compare against any later Sysmon-2 timestomp event.

events.normal_baseline: Constant background volume from browsers writing downloads, applications writing temp/cache files, and normal document editing.

Files dropped by a scripting interpreter (powershell.exe, wscript.exe, mshta.exe) into Temp, AppData, or ProgramData
Double file extensions or extensions that don't match the file's true type, used to disguise an executable
A file created in a system directory by a process not normally responsible for maintaining that directory

attack_example.scenario: A PowerShell downloader writes its retrieved second-stage payload to the Startup folder to survive reboot, immediately after the encoded download command executed.
attack_example.log:
File created:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:05:39.775
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2e13-66f0-4a02-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 9144
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
TargetFilename: C:\Users\k.patel\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\svchost_update.exe
CreationUtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:05:39.775
User: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Check TargetFilename against known autostart, temp, and download locations, weighting executable/script extensions in autostart folders as high priority.
Pull the file's hash (via a subsequent Sysmon-15 stream-hash event or on-disk lookup) and check it against threat intelligence.
Trace ProcessGuid back to the Sysmon-1 event for Image to understand how the file-writing process itself was launched.
false_positives: Legitimate software installers and update mechanisms writing to Startup or Program Files during normal operation
Browser downloads of business-legitimate files that happen to be scripts or executables (installers, tools)

| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 11
| where TargetFilename has "\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\" and TargetFilename has_any (".exe", ".dll", ".ps1", ".vbs", ".lnk")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, TargetFilename, User

Staged multi-part malware delivery
Ransomware precursor payload staging

events.name: RegistryEvent (Object create and delete)
events.description: Logs registry key creation and deletion, distinguished by the EventType field (CreateKey or DeleteKey). Useful for tracking changes to autostart locations and other registry paths malware commonly manipulates.

key_fields.meaning: CreateKey or DeleteKey, identifying which operation occurred.
The full registry key path affected, using Sysmon's abbreviated root names (HKLM, HKU).
The process that performed the registry operation.

events.normal_baseline: Frequent from installers, Windows Update, application configuration writes, and normal system operation creating and cleaning up keys.
events.sample_log:
Registry object added or deleted:
RuleName: -
EventType: CreateKey
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 09:55:03.410
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-3d01-66f0-1401-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 2884
Image: C:\Windows\System32\msiexec.exe
TargetObject: HKLM\SOFTWARE\VendorApp\Settings
User: CORP\jsmith
anomalies: CreateKey under a Run/RunOnce autostart path performed by a scripting interpreter rather than an installer
DeleteKey targeting security-relevant paths such as Windows Defender exclusions or audit policy keys
Registry key creation immediately following a suspicious Sysmon-11 file drop, consistent with registering a new persistence mechanism

attack_example.scenario: Malware creates a new Run key entry pointing at its dropped payload to survive reboot.
attack_example.log:
Registry object added or deleted:
RuleName: -
EventType: CreateKey
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:06:02.550
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2e13-66f0-4a02-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 9144
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
TargetObject: HKU\S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-2201\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\WinUpdateHelper
User: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Check TargetObject against a list of known autostart and security-relevant registry paths (Run/RunOnce, Winlogon, Defender exclusions).
Pivot to the immediately following Sysmon-13 event on the same TargetObject to see the value written into the new key.
Correlate Image and ProcessGuid with the original Sysmon-1 process launch to understand what initiated the registry change.
false_positives: Software installers (msiexec.exe, setup executables) legitimately creating application configuration keys
Windows Update and servicing operations creating and removing keys during patch installation

events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 12
| where EventType == "CreateKey" and TargetObject has_any ("\\Run\\", "\\RunOnce\\", "\\Winlogon\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, TargetObject, User
related_attacks: Registry-based persistence establishment
Defense evasion via Defender exclusion tampering
Malware configuration key creation

events.name: RegistryEvent (Value Set)
events.description: Logs when a registry value is written, recording the actual data for DWORD and QWORD value types in the Details field. This is the event that captures the payload path or command written into an autostart or configuration value.

key_fields.meaning: The full registry value path, with the value name appended after the key path.
The data written to the value; shows the literal number for DWORD/QWORD, otherwise a placeholder for other types.
The process that set the value.

events.normal_baseline: Common during application configuration, Windows Update, and normal settings changes made through the UI or by installers.
events.sample_log:
Registry value set:
RuleName: -
EventType: SetValue
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 09:55:04.001
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-3d01-66f0-1401-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 2884
Image: C:\Windows\System32\msiexec.exe
TargetObject: HKLM\SOFTWARE\VendorApp\Settings\InstallPath
Details: C:\Program Files\VendorApp\
User: CORP\jsmith
anomalies: A Run/RunOnce value written with Details pointing to a script interpreter or a path under Temp/AppData
Details containing an encoded or obfuscated command line rather than a simple path or setting
Value set under security policy or Defender configuration paths that lowers protection (e.g. disabling real-time monitoring)

attack_example.scenario: Malware sets a Run key value to relaunch its dropped executable at every logon, completing the persistence mechanism started in the Sysmon-12 CreateKey event.
attack_example.log:
Registry value set:
RuleName: -
EventType: SetValue
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:06:02.610
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2e13-66f0-4a02-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 9144
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
TargetObject: HKU\S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-2201\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\WinUpdateHelper

User: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Read Details directly to see the exact path or command that will execute; this is often the fastest way to identify the persistence payload.
Check whether TargetObject sits under a Run/RunOnce, Services, or security-policy path that materially changes system behavior.
Cross-reference the path in Details against Sysmon-11 FileCreate events to confirm the referenced file actually exists and when it was dropped.
false_positives: Application installers and updaters writing legitimate configuration values as part of normal setup
Group Policy or configuration-management tools pushing approved registry settings at scale

events.detection_query:

| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 13

Defender/AV configuration tampering for defense evasion

events.name: RegistryEvent (Key and Value Rename)
events.description: Logs registry key and value rename operations, recording the new name via the NewName field. Rarer than create/set events, so an unexpected rename in a sensitive location stands out more clearly.

key_fields.meaning: The original registry key or value path before the rename.
The name the key or value was renamed to.
The process that performed the rename.

events.normal_baseline: Uncommon; occurs mainly during application uninstall/reconfiguration processes that rename their own keys, and some Windows servicing operations.
events.sample_log:

RuleName: -
EventType: RenameKey
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 10:12:00.804
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-4e01-66f0-1501-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 3512
Image: C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe
TargetObject: HKLM\SOFTWARE\VendorApp\Settings.old
NewName: HKLM\SOFTWARE\VendorApp\Settings
User: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
anomalies: A rename operation touching a security-tool or logging-related registry key
Rename performed by a scripting interpreter rather than a legitimate installer or system process
NewName that relocates a value to disguise it under a name resembling a legitimate system key

attack_example.scenario: Malware renames an existing benign-looking registry value to make room before writing its own persistence value under the original name, attempting to blend in.
attack_example.log:
Registry object renamed:
RuleName: -
EventType: RenameKey
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:06:30.442
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2e13-66f0-4a02-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 9144
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
TargetObject: HKU\S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-2201\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\OneDriveSync

User: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Compare TargetObject and NewName to see whether the rename is disguising a takeover of a legitimate-looking value name.
Check what gets written to NewName's original path afterward with a follow-up Sysmon-12/13 event.
Confirm Image is an expected owner of that registry area; a scripting interpreter renaming another vendor's key is unusual.
false_positives: Application updaters that rename old configuration keys as part of a version migration
System component servicing that reorganizes registry structure during a Windows update
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 14
| where TargetObject has_any ("\\Run\\", "\\RunOnce\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, TargetObject, NewName, User

Registry-based evasion of static allowlist checks

events.name: FileCreateStreamHash
events.description: Logs creation of a named alternate data stream and hashes both it and the unnamed (main) stream's contents. Primarily aimed at catching the Zone.Identifier "mark of the web" stream browsers attach to downloaded files, and at malware that hides payloads in ADS.

key_fields.meaning: The file the stream is attached to.
Hash of the file's main content.
The textual contents of the named stream itself, e.g. the Zone.Identifier zone ID and referrer URL.

events.normal_baseline: Generated constantly by normal browser downloads, which attach a Zone.Identifier stream recording the download's source zone and URL.
events.sample_log:
File stream created:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 13:40:02.220
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2c02-66f0-1301-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 4400
Image: C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe
TargetFilename: C:\Users\jsmith\Downloads\quarterly-report.pdf:Zone.Identifier
CreationUtcTime: 2026-09-10 13:40:02.118
Hash: SHA1=0A1B2C3D4E5F60718293A4B5C6D7E8F90A1B2C3
Contents: [ZoneTransfer]\r\nZoneId=3\r\nReferrerUrl=https://mail.contoso-cdn.example/attachments\r\nHostUrl=https://mail.contoso-cdn.example/quarterly-report.pdf
User: CORP\jsmith
anomalies: A downloaded executable carrying ZoneId=3 (internet zone) that then gets executed directly rather than reviewed
Contents referencing a HostUrl or ReferrerUrl on an unrecognized or newly registered domain
A file with data hidden in a named stream with no corresponding Zone.Identifier pattern, consistent with ADS-based payload hiding rather than a browser download

attack_example.scenario: A user downloads a malicious executable disguised as an invoice from a phishing link; the Zone.Identifier stream reveals the true external referring URL.
attack_example.log:
File stream created:

UtcTime: 2026-09-10 13:55:41.310
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2b03-66f0-1601-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 5220
Image: C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe
TargetFilename: C:\Users\k.patel\Downloads\Invoice_0912.exe:Zone.Identifier

Contents: [ZoneTransfer]\r\nZoneId=3\r\nReferrerUrl=http://203.0.113.44/pay/\r\nHostUrl=http://203.0.113.44/pay/Invoice_0912.exe
User: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Extract HostUrl and ReferrerUrl from Contents and check them against threat intelligence and browsing history for the delivery vector.
Confirm whether the underlying TargetFilename (minus the stream suffix) was subsequently executed via a Sysmon-1 event.
For non-Zone.Identifier named streams, treat as higher-priority ADS-hiding activity and inspect Contents directly for embedded payloads.
false_positives: Ordinary browser downloads of legitimate business files, which always carry a Zone.Identifier stream
File transfer or sync tools that preserve zone information when copying downloaded files between locations
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 15
| where TargetFilename has ":Zone.Identifier" and TargetFilename has_any (".exe", ".scr", ".hta", ".js")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, TargetFilename, Contents, User

Alternate data stream payload hiding
SmartScreen/MOTW bypass investigations

events.name: ServiceConfigurationChange
events.description: Logs changes to the Sysmon driver's own configuration, such as when filtering rules are updated via sysmon -c. Detection value is almost entirely about protecting the integrity of Sysmon's own logging rather than catching endpoint attacker behavior.

key_fields.meaning: The configuration change applied, often the command-line arguments or a summary of the new ruleset.
Hash of the configuration XML file used, if one was supplied, allowing detection of unauthorized config swaps.

events.normal_baseline: Fires when Sysmon is installed and whenever an administrator deliberately updates its configuration through approved deployment tooling.
events.sample_log:
Sysmon config state changed:
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 06:15:10.117
Configuration: sysmon64 -c C:\ProgramData\sysmonconfig.xml
ConfigurationFileHash: SHA256=2B4C6E8A0D2F4B6E8A0D2C4E6B8D0F2A4C6E8B0D2F4A6C8E0B2D4F6A8C0E2B4D
anomalies: A ConfigurationFileHash that doesn't match the organization's known-good deployed configuration file hash
A configuration change occurring outside a scheduled deployment window with no corresponding change ticket
A configuration change that immediately precedes reduced logging volume for high-value event types (process access, network connections)

attack_example.scenario: An attacker with local admin rights reconfigures Sysmon to exclude their own tooling's process name from ProcessCreate logging rather than stopping the service outright, a stealthier evasion than a full service stop.
attack_example.log:
Sysmon config state changed:
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:01:00.900
Configuration: sysmon64 -c C:\Users\k.patel\AppData\Local\Temp\quiet.xml
ConfigurationFileHash: SHA256=9F1E3D5C7B9A1D3F5E7C9B1D3F5E7A9C1E3D5F7B9A1C3E5D7F9B1D3E5C7A9F1B

investigation_steps: Compare ConfigurationFileHash against the organization's approved baseline configuration hash for that host's Sysmon deployment.
Check what account and process issued the sysmon -c command via the surrounding Security 4688 or Sysmon-1 events.
If unauthorized, treat any gap or exclusion introduced by the new configuration as a logging blind spot requiring other telemetry to fill.
false_positives: Scheduled Sysmon configuration updates pushed by endpoint management tooling as part of normal maintenance
Version upgrades of Sysmon that reapply or migrate the existing configuration
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 16
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Configuration, ConfigurationFileHash
related_attacks: Stealthy logging-evasion via targeted exclusion rules rather than a full service stop
Attacker tampering with detection tooling ahead of further activity

events.name: PipeEvent (Pipe Created)
events.description: Logs creation of a named pipe, a common interprocess-communication mechanism that malware and post-exploitation frameworks use for local and cross-process control channels, including C2 tooling that tunnels commands over SMB named pipes.

key_fields.meaning: The name of the created named pipe; many attacker frameworks use recognizable or randomly generated pipe name patterns.
The process that created the pipe.

events.normal_baseline: Common from legitimate Windows services, print spooler, RPC-based applications, and management tools that use named pipes for normal IPC.
events.sample_log:
Pipe Created:
RuleName: -
EventType: CreatePipe
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 11:20:04.008
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-5e02-66f0-1701-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 1200
PipeName: \lsarpc
Image: C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe
anomalies: A pipe name matching a known post-exploitation framework's default or randomized pattern (e.g. MSSE- prefixed or short hex-string names)
A pipe created by a scripting interpreter or LOLBin rather than a system service
High-frequency creation of uniquely-named pipes from the same process in a short window

attack_example.scenario: A Cobalt Strike-style beacon creates a named pipe with a default-looking randomized name to relay commands between its SMB beacon and a spawned child process.
attack_example.log:
Pipe Created:
RuleName: -
EventType: CreatePipe
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:07:15.660
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2e13-66f0-4a02-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 9144
PipeName: \MSSE-6204-server
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe

investigation_steps: Check PipeName against known malicious/default C2 framework pipe-name patterns and against a baseline of pipe names normal for this host.
Correlate with the immediately following Sysmon-18 PipeConnected event to see which process connected to the pipe.
Review Image's parent chain and command line via Sysmon-1 to establish how the pipe-creating process was launched.
false_positives: Standard Windows RPC, print spooler, and named-pipe-based services operating normally
Legitimate remote administration tools (PsExec, WinRM backends) that use named pipes for their normal function
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 17
| where PipeName matches regex @"\\(MSSE-|status_|[a-f0-9]{6,}$)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, PipeName
related_attacks: Cobalt Strike and similar C2 named-pipe communication
PsExec-based lateral movement
Post-exploitation frameworks using named pipes for local privilege escalation

events.name: PipeEvent (Pipe Connected)
events.description: Logs when a client connects to an existing named pipe, complementing Sysmon-17 by identifying which process consumed the pipe rather than just which one created it.

key_fields.meaning: The named pipe being connected to.
The client process making the connection.

events.normal_baseline: Occurs alongside every legitimate PipeCreate event as normal client-server IPC completes its handshake.
events.sample_log:
Pipe Connected:
RuleName: -
EventType: ConnectPipe
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 11:20:04.031
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-5f03-66f0-1801-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 1420
PipeName: \lsarpc
Image: C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe
anomalies: A client process connecting to a pipe with a name matching a known C2 framework pattern
An unusual client Image connecting to a pipe normally only consumed by a specific system service
Pipe connect events with no corresponding PipeCreate event in the retained log, suggesting a gap or cross-host pipe access

attack_example.scenario: A second beacon-spawned process connects to the named pipe set up by the initial implant to receive relayed commands, completing the local C2 relay chain.
attack_example.log:
Pipe Connected:
RuleName: -
EventType: ConnectPipe
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:07:16.010
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-3f14-66f0-4b03-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 3388
PipeName: \MSSE-6204-server
Image: C:\Windows\System32\rundll32.exe

investigation_steps: Pair with the corresponding Sysmon-17 event on the same PipeName to establish the full creator-to-consumer relationship.
Check whether the connecting Image is a process type that has any legitimate reason to talk to the pipe's owning service.
If the pipe name matches a known C2 pattern, treat both the creating and connecting processes as compromised and scope accordingly.
false_positives: Normal RPC client-server handshakes between legitimate Windows services
Administrative tools connecting to management pipes during routine remote operations
events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 18
| where PipeName matches regex @"\\(MSSE-|status_|[a-f0-9]{6,}$)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, PipeName

Lateral movement tooling connecting to service-control pipes

events.name: WmiEvent (WmiEventFilter activity detected)
events.description: Logs registration of a WMI event filter, the trigger-condition half of a WMI permanent event subscription. Filter registration is a well-documented fileless persistence technique that survives reboots without leaving a file on disk.

key_fields.meaning: The name given to the WMI event filter.
The WQL query defining the trigger condition, e.g. a logon event or a timer interval.
The WMI namespace the filter is registered in, typically root\subscription.

events.normal_baseline: Rare in normal operation; legitimate uses include some enterprise monitoring and management software that relies on WMI eventing.
events.sample_log:
WmiEventFilter activity detected:
RuleName: -
EventType: WmiFilterEvent
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 15:00:02.410
Operation: Created
User: CORP\svc_mgmt
EventNamespace: root\subscription
Name: SCCM-HealthCheck-Filter
Query: SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHIN 60 WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_Processor'
anomalies: A filter Name that mimics a legitimate-sounding label but registered by an account or process with no management-tool history
A Query condition tied to logon events, system idle, or startup, common triggers for fileless malware persistence
Filter registration occurring shortly after a suspicious PowerShell or scripting process execution

attack_example.scenario: An attacker registers a WMI event filter that triggers on user logon, the first half of a fileless persistence mechanism that will later execute a payload via a bound consumer.
attack_example.log:
WmiEventFilter activity detected:
RuleName: -
EventType: WmiFilterEvent
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:30:00.115
Operation: Created
User: CORP\k.patel
EventNamespace: root\subscription
Name: UpdateCheckFilter
Query: SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHIN 5 WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_LogonSession' AND TargetInstance.LogonType = 2

investigation_steps: Read the Query field directly to understand exactly what condition will trigger the bound consumer.
Check User and the surrounding Sysmon-1 process activity for what created the filter; unexpected accounts or scripting interpreters are high priority.
Immediately pull the matching Sysmon-21 WmiEventConsumerToFilter event to identify which consumer this filter is bound to and what it executes.
false_positives: Enterprise systems-management software (SCCM, monitoring agents) that legitimately uses WMI permanent event subscriptions
Custom internal automation built by IT that relies on WMI eventing for legitimate health checks

attack_techniques.name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription

events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 19
| where Operation == "Created"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, User, Name, Query, EventNamespace
related_attacks: Fileless WMI-based persistence
Living-off-the-land malware avoiding disk artifacts
Post-compromise persistence surviving reboots without a scheduled task or Run key

events.name: WmiEvent (WmiEventConsumer activity detected)
events.description: Logs registration of a WMI event consumer, the action half of a WMI permanent event subscription that defines what actually executes when the paired filter's condition is met. CommandLineEventConsumer and ActiveScriptEventConsumer types are the ones most commonly abused for code execution.

key_fields.meaning: The name of the registered consumer.
The consumer class, e.g. CommandLineEventConsumer or ActiveScriptEventConsumer, which determines what kind of action it performs.
The command line or script the consumer executes when triggered.

events.normal_baseline: Rare; legitimate management and monitoring tools occasionally register consumers, but most endpoints see none in normal operation.
events.sample_log:
WmiEventConsumer activity detected:
RuleName: -
EventType: WmiConsumerEvent
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 15:00:03.660
Operation: Created
User: CORP\svc_mgmt
Name: SCCM-HealthCheck-Consumer
Type: CommandLineEventConsumer
Destination: C:\Windows\CCM\HealthCheck.exe -run
anomalies: Type of CommandLineEventConsumer or ActiveScriptEventConsumer with a Destination pointing at PowerShell, cmd.exe, or an encoded script
Destination referencing a file in Temp or AppData rather than a Program Files install location
Consumer creation immediately following a suspicious Sysmon-19 filter registration from the same user context

attack_example.scenario: The attacker binds a CommandLineEventConsumer to the earlier logon-triggered filter, so every future logon re-launches their payload without any file needing to run at startup through conventional means.
attack_example.log:
WmiEventConsumer activity detected:
RuleName: -
EventType: WmiConsumerEvent
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:30:00.410
Operation: Created
User: CORP\k.patel
Name: UpdateCheckConsumer
Type: CommandLineEventConsumer
Destination: powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0ATwBiAGoAZQBjAHQAIABOAGUAdAAuAFcAZQBiAEMAbABpAGUAbgB0ACkA

investigation_steps: Read Destination directly; a CommandLineEventConsumer's destination is the exact command that will run on trigger, decode any Base64 present.
Match Name against the corresponding Sysmon-19 filter and Sysmon-21 binding to reconstruct the complete persistence chain.
Remove the consumer and filter via WMI cleanup tooling once confirmed malicious, since standard antivirus scans often miss WMI-resident persistence.
false_positives: Legitimate systems-management platforms that register command-line consumers for health checks or inventory scripts
Custom internal automation using WMI eventing as an intentional design choice

attack_techniques.name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription

events.detection_query:
Event
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 20
| where Type in ("CommandLineEventConsumer", "ActiveScriptEventConsumer")
| where Destination has_any ("powershell", "cmd.exe", "-enc", "\\Temp\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, User, Name, Type, Destination
related_attacks: Fileless WMI-based persistence execution
Living-off-the-land command execution surviving reboot
Advanced persistent threat backdoor mechanisms avoiding scheduled tasks

events.name: WmiEvent (WmiEventConsumerToFilter activity detected)
events.description: Logs the binding operation that links a WMI event consumer to an event filter, completing a permanent event subscription. This is the final piece needed to confirm a full WMI persistence chain is active and armed.

key_fields.meaning: The consumer being bound, identified by its class and name.
The filter being bound, identified by its namespace and name.

events.normal_baseline: Rare; occurs only when a filter and consumer pair are actively linked, which most endpoints never do outside specific management software.
events.sample_log:
WmiEventConsumerToFilter activity detected:
RuleName: -
EventType: WmiBindingEvent
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 15:00:03.712
Operation: Created
User: CORP\svc_mgmt
Consumer: CommandLineEventConsumer=SCCM-HealthCheck-Consumer
Filter: root\subscription:SCCM-HealthCheck-Filter
anomalies: A binding event with no legitimate management software context for either the Consumer or Filter names
Binding created by a user account or process outside the normal WMI-management tooling baseline
Binding completing within seconds of the corresponding Sysmon-19 and Sysmon-20 events from the same session, a full persistence chain assembled in one short burst

attack_example.scenario: The final binding step activates the earlier logon-triggered filter and its command-line consumer, arming a complete fileless persistence mechanism.
attack_example.log:

events.name: DNSEvent (DNS query)
events.description: Logs DNS queries made by any process, whether they succeed, fail, or resolve from cache, tying each lookup directly to the requesting process. Not available on Windows 7 and earlier; requires the DNS query telemetry introduced with Windows 8.1.

key_fields.meaning: The domain name being resolved.
The result status code; 0 means success, nonzero values indicate failure or NXDOMAIN.
The resolved IP address(es) and record type returned, when the query succeeded.
The process that issued the DNS query.

events.normal_baseline: Extremely high volume; every application, browser tab, and background service issues DNS queries as part of normal network activity.
events.sample_log:
Dns query:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 10:44:11.850
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-4b02-66f0-2201-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 7712
QueryName: www.contoso-cdn.example
QueryStatus: 0
QueryResults: type: 5 cdn.contoso-cdn.example;::ffff:203.0.113.10;
Image: C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe
User: CORP\jsmith
anomalies: QueryName consisting of long, high-entropy random-looking subdomains, consistent with DNS tunneling or a domain generation algorithm
A LOLBin or scripting interpreter (powershell.exe, rundll32.exe) issuing DNS queries directly rather than a browser or known network-facing app
A high volume of distinct QueryName lookups from the same Image in a short window, consistent with DGA-based C2 domain rotation
QueryStatus consistently nonzero for a long sequence of similar-looking domains, suggesting the client is cycling through DGA candidates

attack_example.scenario: An implant uses DNS as a low-and-slow C2 channel, issuing queries for encoded subdomains of an attacker-controlled domain to exfiltrate data a few bytes at a time.
attack_example.log:
Dns query:
RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:08:20.115
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-2e13-66f0-4a02-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 9144
QueryName: 7a1f9c3d5e2b8f01.updates.example-tunnel.com
QueryStatus: 0
QueryResults: type: 1 198.51.100.77;
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
User: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Check QueryName for high entropy, unusual length, or a DGA-like pattern, and compare the requesting Image against expected DNS-issuing processes.
Aggregate QueryName volume per Image and per parent domain over time to spot tunneling or DGA rotation that a single query wouldn't reveal.
Cross-reference the resolved QueryResults IP against the same host's Sysmon-3 network connections to confirm whether a connection followed the lookup.
false_positives: CDN and cloud service domains that legitimately use long, semi-random subdomain labels
Ad-tech and telemetry SDKs embedded in legitimate applications that generate high query volume to varied subdomains

events.name: FileDelete (File Delete archived)

key_fields.meaning: The file that was deleted.
Hash of the deleted file's content, computed before archival.
True if the deleted file was a PE executable, a strong prioritization signal.
Whether the file's content was successfully preserved in the ArchiveDirectory.

events.normal_baseline: Common from temp-file cleanup, installer post-install removal of setup files, and normal user file management.

Hash of the archived clipboard content, useful only for matching against a known content hash, not for reading the content itself.
Whether the clipboard content was saved to the archive directory.

events.name: ProcessTampering
events.description: Detects process image tampering techniques such as process hollowing and process herpaderping, where a process's in-memory image is manipulated to run different code than what's on disk or what Windows originally mapped. This is a low-volume, high-fidelity event: legitimate software essentially never does this.

key_fields.meaning: The kind of tampering detected, e.g. "Image is replaced", indicating the process's mapped image no longer matches what was originally loaded.
The tampered process.
Ties this tampering event to the process's original Sysmon-1 creation event.

events.normal_baseline: Effectively none; legitimate software has almost no reason to replace or hollow out its own running process image.

RuleName: -
UtcTime: 2026-09-10 14:16:00.220
ProcessGuid: {5d3a2c91-7a01-66f0-1101-000000000a00}
ProcessId: 2244
Image: C:\Windows\System32\notepad.exe
Type: Image is replaced
User: CORP\k.patel
anomalies: Any occurrence of this event on a standard, non-development endpoint is inherently suspicious given how rare legitimate triggers are
Type: Image is replaced occurring shortly after a Sysmon-8 CreateRemoteThread event targeting the same ProcessGuid
A tampered process that subsequently makes network connections or accesses credentials inconsistent with its apparent identity

ProcessId: 2244
Image: C:\Windows\System32\notepad.exe
Type: Image is replaced
User: CORP\k.patel

investigation_steps: Treat this event as high-confidence malicious by default and immediately pull the full process history for ProcessGuid, including its Sysmon-1 launch and any Sysmon-8/Sysmon-10 events touching it.
Capture a memory image of the affected process if still running, since the on-disk file will look benign while memory holds the actual payload.
Check what launched the now-tampered process and whether that launcher is itself part of the same attack chain.
false_positives: Certain legitimate application packers, updaters, or anti-cheat/DRM software that self-modify their own process image (rare and should be explicitly allowlisted)

events.name: FileBlockExecutable

key_fields.meaning: The executable file path Sysmon blocked from being written.
The process that attempted to create the blocked file.
Hash computed on the blocked file content before the write was denied.

events.normal_baseline: Should be rare to nonexistent in a well-tuned environment; every occurrence represents a write that matched an explicit block rule and was prevented.

anomalies: Any block event is itself the anomaly signal; investigate every occurrence rather than trying to filter noise out of it
Repeated block attempts for slightly varied file names or paths from the same Image, indicating an attacker retrying to bypass the block
A block on a file whose hash matches a known-malicious sample already in threat intelligence
